text:
A car accelerates uniformly from $4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $16.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in $6.0\ \text{s}$. What is the distance travelled by the car in this time?

A. $48\ \text{m}$
B. $60\ \text{m}$
C. $72\ \text{m}$
D. $96\ \text{m}$
ms: $s = \frac{(u+v)}{2}t = \frac{4.0+16.0}{2}\times 6.0 = 60\ \text{m}$. A ignores the initial speed ($\frac{1}{2}\times 16\times 6$); C adds $ut$ to $\frac{1}{2}vt$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}(v-u)t$; D uses the final speed for the whole time.

text:
The graph shows how the velocity of a cyclist varies with time over $10\ \text{s}$.

![velocity-time graph: 0 to 12 m/s in 4 s, constant to 8 s, then down to zero at 10 s](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.1_2.svg)

What is the average speed of the cyclist over the $10\ \text{s}$?

A. $6.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
B. $7.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
C. $8.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
D. $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
ms: Distance = area under the graph $= \frac{1}{2}(4)(12) + (4)(12) + \frac{1}{2}(2)(12) = 24 + 48 + 12 = 84\ \text{m}$, so average speed $= 84/10 = 8.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. A averages only the maximum and minimum speeds; D is the maximum speed, not the average.

text:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. What are the velocity and the acceleration of the ball at its highest point?

A. velocity zero, acceleration zero
B. velocity zero, acceleration $g$ downwards
C. velocity maximum, acceleration zero
D. velocity zero, acceleration $g$ upwards
ms: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, but the only force acting is still its weight, so the acceleration is $g$ downwards throughout. A is the common misconception that zero velocity means zero acceleration.

text:
A stone is thrown horizontally at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a vertical cliff $20\ \text{m}$ high. Air resistance is negligible and $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. What is the horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff to where the stone lands?

A. $15\ \text{m}$
B. $20\ \text{m}$
C. $30\ \text{m}$
D. $61\ \text{m}$
ms: Vertical: $20 = \frac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2.02\ \text{s}$. Horizontal: $x = 15 \times 2.02 = 30\ \text{m}$. D uses $t^2$ ($4.08$) in place of $t$; A assumes a time of 1 s.

text:
Ball X is released from rest at a height $h$ above the ground. At the same instant ball Y is projected vertically upwards from the ground directly below X with speed $u$. Air resistance is negligible. The balls collide in mid-air. How long after release do they collide?

A. $\dfrac{h}{u}$
B. $\dfrac{2h}{u}$
C. $\dfrac{h}{2u}$
D. $\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$
ms: Both balls have the same acceleration $g$, so relative to X, ball Y moves at a constant speed $u$ and must close a gap $h$: $t = h/u$ (equivalently $h - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = ut - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$). D is the time for X to reach the ground alone; B and C are algebra slips.

text:
A skydiver falls from rest. Air resistance increases with speed and the skydiver eventually reaches terminal speed. Which statements are correct about the motion before terminal speed is reached?

I. The acceleration decreases from $g$ towards zero.
II. The velocity increases at a decreasing rate.
III. The resultant force on the skydiver is constant.

A. I only
B. I and II only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: As speed increases, drag increases, so the resultant force (weight minus drag) and hence the acceleration fall from $g$ to zero: I and II are correct. III is wrong because the resultant force decreases.

text:
A student investigates the motion of a trolley released from rest on an inclined track. The distance $s$ travelled by the trolley in time $t$ is measured. The uncertainty in each time measurement is $\pm 0.05\ \text{s}$; the uncertainty in $s$ is negligible.

| $t$ / s | $s$ / m |
|---|---|
| 0.50 | 0.11 |
| 1.00 | 0.39 |
| 1.50 | 0.92 |
| 2.00 | 1.58 |
| 2.50 | 2.51 |

(a) Calculate the absolute uncertainty in $t^2$ for $t = 2.00\ \text{s}$. [2]

The student plots a graph of $s$ against $t^2$ with a line of best fit.

![graph of s against t squared with error bars and a straight line of best fit through the origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.1_7.svg)

(b) Determine the acceleration of the trolley using the graph. [3]

(c) Explain how the graph supports the hypothesis that the trolley moves with uniform acceleration from rest. [2]

(d) The times were measured with a hand-held stopwatch. Suggest one change to the method that would reduce the uncertainty in $t$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- fractional uncertainty in $t$ $= \frac{0.05}{2.00} = 0.025$ (2.5 %), so fractional uncertainty in $t^2$ = $2 \times 0.025 = 0.050$ ✓
- $\Delta(t^2) = 0.050 \times 4.00 = \pm 0.20\ \text{s}^2$ ✓

(b)
- gradient calculated from two well-separated points on the line, e.g. $\frac{2.70 - 0}{6.75 - 0} \approx 0.40\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓
- recognition that $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$ so gradient $= \frac{a}{2}$ ✓
- $a = 2 \times 0.40 \approx 0.80\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓
- Accept gradient 0.38–0.42 and $a$ in the range 0.76–0.84 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Award [1 max] for $a = $ gradient (factor of 2 missing).

(c)
- the graph of $s$ against $t^2$ is a straight line (all points/error bars lie on it), so $s \propto t^2$ ✓
- the line passes through the origin, consistent with $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$ and constant $a$ ✓

(d)
- use light gates / data logger / motion sensor / video analysis with a frame-by-frame timer
- OR repeat each timing several times and average ✓
- Accept any one valid suggestion.

text:
A driver is travelling at $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when she sees an obstacle ahead. Her reaction time is $0.70\ \text{s}$. After she applies the brakes, the car decelerates uniformly at $6.25\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ until it stops.

(a) Calculate the distance travelled during the reaction time. [1]

(b) Calculate the braking distance. [2]

(c) State the total stopping distance. [1]

(d) Sketch a velocity–time graph for the car from the moment she sees the obstacle until the car stops. Label the key values on both axes. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $25 \times 0.70 = 17.5\ \text{m}$ ✓

(b)
- use of $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $0 = 25^2 - 2(6.25)s$ ✓
- $s = 50\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- $17.5 + 50 = 67.5\ \text{m}$ (allow ECF from (a) and (b)) ✓

(d)
- horizontal line at $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.70\ \text{s}$ ✓
- straight line falling to zero at $t = 0.70 + \frac{25}{6.25} = 4.7\ \text{s}$ ✓

text:
A ball is kicked from level ground with a speed of $18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $35^\circ$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity. [2]

(b) Calculate the maximum height reached by the ball. [2]

(c) A wall of height $2.5\ \text{m}$ stands $25\ \text{m}$ horizontally from the point where the ball is kicked. Determine whether the ball passes over the wall. [3]

(d) In reality air resistance is not negligible. State and explain the effect of air resistance on the maximum height of the ball. [2]
ms:
(a)
- horizontal: $18\cos 35^\circ = 14.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
- vertical: $18\sin 35^\circ = 10.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(b)
- $0 = 10.3^2 - 2(9.8)h$ ✓
- $h = 5.4\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- time to reach the wall $t = \frac{25}{14.7} = 1.70\ \text{s}$ ✓
- height at that time $y = 10.3(1.70) - \frac{1}{2}(9.8)(1.70)^2 = 3.4\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $3.4\ \text{m} > 2.5\ \text{m}$ so the ball passes over the wall ✓
- Allow ECF from (a). The conclusion must be supported by a calculated height (or by comparing times).

(d)
- maximum height is reduced ✓
- air resistance acts downwards (opposite to the velocity) on the way up, so the upward deceleration is greater than $g$ / some kinetic energy is transferred to the air (thermal energy) ✓

text:
An object starts from rest at $t = 0$ and moves in a straight line. The graph shows how its acceleration varies with time.

![acceleration-time graph: 2.0 from 0 to 4 s, zero from 4 to 7 s, -4.0 from 7 to 9 s](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.1_10.svg)

(a) Determine the velocity of the object at $t = 4.0\ \text{s}$. [1]

(b) Determine the velocity of the object at $t = 9.0\ \text{s}$. [1]

(c) Sketch a velocity–time graph for the object from $t = 0$ to $t = 9.0\ \text{s}$. [2]

(d) Calculate the total displacement of the object from $t = 0$ to $t = 9.0\ \text{s}$. [3]

(e) Calculate the average velocity of the object over the $9.0\ \text{s}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- area under $a$–$t$ graph: $v = 2.0 \times 4.0 = 8.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(b)
- $v = 8.0 - 4.0 \times 2.0 = 0$ ✓

(c)
- straight line from origin to $8.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 4 s, then horizontal to 7 s ✓
- straight line from $8.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 7 s down to zero at 9 s ✓

(d)
- 0–4 s: $\frac{1}{2}(4.0)(8.0) = 16\ \text{m}$ ✓
- 4–7 s: $8.0 \times 3.0 = 24\ \text{m}$ and 7–9 s: $\frac{1}{2}(2.0)(8.0) = 8.0\ \text{m}$ ✓
- total $= 48\ \text{m}$ ✓
- Award [3] for a correct final answer. Allow ECF from (c).

(e)
- $\frac{48}{9.0} = 5.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (ECF from (d)) ✓

text:
A stone is thrown vertically upwards at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the edge of a vertical cliff. The stone rises, then falls past the cliff edge and lands at the foot of the cliff, $30\ \text{m}$ below the point of release. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the time taken for the stone to reach its highest point. [1]

(b) Calculate the maximum height of the stone above the point of release. [1]

(c) Show that the stone lands about $4.0\ \text{s}$ after it is thrown. [2]

(d) Calculate the speed of the stone as it lands. [2]

(e) A second stone is released from rest at the cliff edge at the instant the first stone passes the cliff edge on its way down. Determine which stone lands first and the time interval between the two landings. [3]
ms:
(a)
- $t = \frac{12}{9.8} = 1.2\ \text{s}$ ✓

(b)
- $h = \frac{12^2}{2 \times 9.8} = 7.3\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- taking upwards as positive: $-30 = 12t - 4.9t^2$ ✓
- $4.9t^2 - 12t - 30 = 0 \Rightarrow t = \frac{12 + \sqrt{144 + 588}}{9.8} = 3.99\ \text{s} \approx 4.0\ \text{s}$ ✓
- Answer given; the working must be shown. Alternative: 1.22 s up, then fall of $37.3\ \text{m}$ from rest taking 2.76 s.

(d)
- $v^2 = 12^2 + 2(9.8)(30)$ ✓
- $v = 27\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(e)
- first stone passes the edge at $t = 2 \times 1.22 = 2.45\ \text{s}$ moving downwards at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so it lands $3.99 - 2.45 = 1.54\ \text{s}$ later ✓
- second stone: $30 = \frac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2.47\ \text{s}$ ✓
- first stone lands first, by $2.47 - 1.54 = 0.94\ \text{s}$ ✓
- Accept 0.9 s. Allow ECF from (c).

text:
A book rests on a horizontal table. According to Newton's third law, which force forms a pair with the weight of the book?

A. The normal force of the table on the book
B. The gravitational force of the book on the Earth
C. The force of the book on the table
D. The friction force of the table on the book
ms: Newton's third-law pairs are the same type of force acting on different bodies: Earth pulls the book down (weight), the book pulls Earth up. A is equal and opposite but acts on the same body (equilibrium, not a third-law pair); C pairs with A.

text:
A block of mass $2.0\ \text{kg}$ slides down a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The block moves at constant velocity. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

![block of mass 2.0 kg sliding down a plane inclined at 30 degrees](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.2_2.svg)

What is the magnitude of the frictional force on the block?

A. $0\ \text{N}$
B. $9.8\ \text{N}$
C. $17\ \text{N}$
D. $20\ \text{N}$
ms: Constant velocity means zero resultant force, so friction balances the component of weight along the plane: $mg\sin 30^\circ = 2.0 \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = 9.8\ \text{N}$. C uses $mg\cos 30^\circ$ (which equals the normal force); D is the whole weight; A assumes no force is needed for constant velocity.

text:
A person of mass $60\ \text{kg}$ stands in a lift that is accelerating upwards at $2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. What is the normal force of the lift floor on the person?

A. $468\ \text{N}$
B. $588\ \text{N}$
C. $708\ \text{N}$
D. $120\ \text{N}$
ms: $N - mg = ma \Rightarrow N = 60(9.8 + 2.0) = 708\ \text{N}$. A is for a downward acceleration; B is the weight (lift at rest or constant velocity); D is only the resultant force $ma$.

text:
A trolley of mass $2.0\ \text{kg}$ moving at $3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides with a stationary trolley of mass $1.0\ \text{kg}$. The trolleys stick together. What is the loss of kinetic energy in the collision?

A. $0\ \text{J}$
B. $3.0\ \text{J}$
C. $6.0\ \text{J}$
D. $9.0\ \text{J}$
ms: Momentum: $2.0 \times 3.0 = 3.0v \Rightarrow v = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $E_k$ before $= \frac{1}{2}(2.0)(3.0)^2 = 9.0\ \text{J}$; after $= \frac{1}{2}(3.0)(2.0)^2 = 6.0\ \text{J}$; loss $= 3.0\ \text{J}$. C is the final kinetic energy, D the initial; A assumes kinetic energy is conserved, which is true only for elastic collisions.

text:
A ball of mass $0.15\ \text{kg}$ travels horizontally at $8.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards a bat. The graph shows how the force exerted on the ball by the bat varies with time. The force acts in the direction opposite to the ball's initial velocity.

![force-time graph: triangle rising to 120 N at 25 ms and back to zero at 50 ms](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.2_5.svg)

What is the speed of the ball when it leaves the bat?

A. $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
B. $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
C. $28\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
D. $32\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
ms: Impulse = area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.050)(120) = 3.0\ \text{N s}$. Taking the bat's force as positive: $p_{\text{final}} = -0.15 \times 8.0 + 3.0 = 1.8\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$, so $v = 12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. B ignores the initial momentum; C adds it with the wrong sign; D omits the $\frac{1}{2}$ in the triangle area (impulse taken as $6.0\ \text{N s}$).

text:
A small ball of mass $m$ is attached to a light inextensible string and moves in a vertical circle. Air resistance is negligible. What is the difference between the tension in the string at the lowest point and the tension at the highest point of the circle?

A. $2mg$
B. $4mg$
C. $6mg$
D. It depends on the speed of the ball.
ms: Lowest: $T_L - mg = mv_L^2/r$; highest: $T_H + mg = mv_H^2/r$; energy: $v_L^2 = v_H^2 + 4gr$. So $T_L - T_H = 2mg + m(v_L^2 - v_H^2)/r = 2mg + 4mg = 6mg$, independent of speed. A ignores the change in speed; D is the tempting but wrong guess.

text:
A student investigates static friction between a wooden block and a horizontal bench. Masses are added to the block to change the normal force $N$. A force sensor pulls the block horizontally and records the maximum force $F_{\text{max}}$ before the block starts to slide. The uncertainty in $F_{\text{max}}$ is $\pm 0.2\ \text{N}$; the uncertainty in $N$ is negligible.

| $N$ / N | $F_{\text{max}}$ / N |
|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.9 |
| 4.0 | 1.7 |
| 6.0 | 2.6 |
| 8.0 | 3.3 |
| 10.0 | 4.2 |

![graph of maximum friction force against normal force with error bars and line of best fit](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.2_7.svg)

(a) Suggest why the line of best fit is expected to pass through the origin. [1]

(b) Determine the coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$ between the block and the bench. [2]

(c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $F_{\text{max}}$ when $N = 4.0\ \text{N}$. [1]

(d) The student wants to measure the coefficient of dynamic friction $\mu_d$. Outline how the method could be changed to do this. [2]

(e) Estimate $F_{\text{max}}$ when $N = 15\ \text{N}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $F_{\text{max}} = \mu_s N$, so when $N = 0$ there is no friction / $F_{\text{max}} \propto N$ ✓

(b)
- gradient of line from two well-separated points, e.g. $\frac{4.59 - 0.08}{11 - 0}$ ✓
- $\mu_s = 0.41$ ✓
- Accept 0.38–0.44. No unit; penalize a unit.

(c)
- $\frac{0.2}{1.7} \times 100 = 12\ \%$ ✓

(d)
- pull the block so that it slides at constant velocity (zero acceleration) ✓
- record the (steady) force while sliding; then $\mu_d = F/N$ / plot $F$ against $N$ and use the gradient ✓

(e)
- $F_{\text{max}} \approx 0.41 \times 15 \approx 6.2\ \text{N}$ ✓
- Accept 6.0–6.6 N (extrapolation of the line or $\mu_s N$).

text:
A box of mass $12\ \text{kg}$ is pulled across a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of $50\ \text{N}$. The coefficient of dynamic friction between the box and the floor is $0.30$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing the forces acting on the box. [2]

(b) Calculate the frictional force on the box. [1]

(c) Calculate the acceleration of the box. [2]

(d) The $50\ \text{N}$ force is now applied at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Explain why the frictional force on the box decreases. [2]
ms:
(a)
- four forces drawn from the box: weight down, normal reaction up, applied force horizontally forwards, friction horizontally backwards ✓
- all correctly labelled, with weight and normal force of similar length ✓

![expected free-body diagram: normal reaction up, weight down, 50 N pull right, friction left](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.2_8-ms.svg)

(b)
- $F_f = \mu_d N = 0.30 \times 12 \times 9.8 = 35\ \text{N}$ ✓

(c)
- $F_{\text{net}} = 50 - 35.3 = 14.7\ \text{N}$ ✓
- $a = \frac{14.7}{12} = 1.2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- the applied force now has an upward vertical component ($50\sin 30^\circ = 25\ \text{N}$), so the normal force is reduced (to about 93 N) ✓
- friction $= \mu_d N$ is proportional to the normal force, so friction decreases ✓

text:
Block A of mass $3.0\ \text{kg}$ rests on a horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley to block B of mass $1.0\ \text{kg}$, which hangs freely. The system is released from rest. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

![block A on a table connected by a string over a pulley at the edge to hanging block B](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.2_9.svg)

Initially the table is frictionless.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the blocks. [2]

(b) Calculate the tension in the string. [2]

(c) Explain why the tension in the string is less than the weight of block B. [1]

The experiment is repeated with a rough table. The coefficient of dynamic friction between A and the table is $0.20$.

(d) Calculate the new acceleration of the blocks. [2]
ms:
(a)
- resultant force on system $= m_B g = 9.8\ \text{N}$, total mass $= 4.0\ \text{kg}$ ✓
- $a = \frac{9.8}{4.0} = 2.45 \approx 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓

(b)
- for A: $T = m_A a$ (or for B: $m_B g - T = m_B a$) ✓
- $T = 3.0 \times 2.45 = 7.4\ \text{N}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- B accelerates downwards so there must be a resultant downward force on B, hence $T < m_B g$ ✓

(d)
- friction on A $= 0.20 \times 3.0 \times 9.8 = 5.88\ \text{N}$ ✓
- $a = \frac{9.8 - 5.88}{4.0} = 0.98\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ ✓

text:
A car of mass $900\ \text{kg}$ drives at a constant speed of $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ over a bridge whose road surface is part of a vertical circle of radius $25\ \text{m}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Explain why the car is accelerating even though its speed is constant. [2]

(b) Calculate the normal force exerted by the road on the car at the top of the bridge. [2]

(c) Calculate the maximum speed at which the car can pass over the top of the bridge without losing contact with the road. [2]

(d) Later the car travels round a horizontal unbanked bend of radius $40\ \text{m}$. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is $0.60$. Determine the maximum speed at which the car can take the bend without skidding. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the direction of the velocity is changing, so the velocity changes ✓
- acceleration is the rate of change of velocity / there is a centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre of the circle ✓

(b)
- $mg - N = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ ✓
- $N = 900\left(9.8 - \frac{144}{25}\right) = 3.6 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$ ✓

(c)
- contact is lost when $N = 0$, so $mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{9.8 \times 25} = 16\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept 15.7)

(d)
- maximum friction provides the centripetal force: $\mu_s mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{0.60 \times 9.8 \times 40} = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept 15.3)

text:
A firework of mass $0.60\ \text{kg}$ is moving horizontally at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at the top of its flight when it explodes into two pieces. Immediately after the explosion, a piece of mass $0.20\ \text{kg}$ moves horizontally at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the direction opposite to the original motion. Ignore any mass lost in the explosion and the effect of gravity during the explosion.

(a) State the condition under which the total momentum of a system is conserved. [1]

(b) Determine the velocity of the other piece immediately after the explosion. [2]

(c) Calculate the kinetic energy released in the explosion. [3]

(d) The explosion lasts $2.0\ \text{ms}$. Calculate the magnitude of the average force on the $0.20\ \text{kg}$ piece during the explosion. [2]

(e) State, with a reason, the magnitude of the average force on the other piece during the explosion. [1]
ms:
(a)
- no resultant external force acts on the system / the system is isolated ✓

(b)
- $0.60 \times 20 = 0.20 \times (-10) + 0.40v$ ✓
- $v = 35\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the original direction of motion ✓

(c)
- initial $E_k = \frac{1}{2}(0.60)(20)^2 = 120\ \text{J}$ ✓
- final $E_k = \frac{1}{2}(0.20)(10)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(0.40)(35)^2 = 10 + 245 = 255\ \text{J}$ ✓
- energy released $= 135\ \text{J}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- $\Delta p = 0.20 \times (-10 - 20) = -6.0\ \text{N s}$ ✓
- $F = \frac{6.0}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.0 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$ ✓

(e)
- $3.0 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$, because by Newton's third law the pieces exert equal and opposite forces on each other (also its momentum change is $0.40 \times 15 = 6.0\ \text{N s}$) ✓

text:
A steel sphere of radius $2.0\ \text{mm}$ is released in a tall cylinder of oil. It quickly reaches a terminal speed of $0.080\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Density of steel $= 7.8 \times 10^3\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$; density of oil $= 9.0 \times 10^2\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Identify the three forces acting on the sphere when it moves at terminal speed and state the relationship between them. [2]

(b) Determine the viscosity of the oil. [3]

(c) A steel sphere of radius $4.0\ \text{mm}$ is released in the same oil. Predict its terminal speed. Assume that Stokes' law still applies. [2]
ms:
(a)
- weight (downwards), buoyancy/upthrust (upwards) and viscous drag (upwards) ✓
- weight = buoyancy + drag (resultant force zero) ✓

(b)
- $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi(2.0 \times 10^{-3})^3 = 3.35 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{m}^3$ ✓
- weight − buoyancy $= (7800 - 900)(3.35 \times 10^{-8})(9.8) = 2.27 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$ ✓
- $\eta = \frac{2.27 \times 10^{-3}}{6\pi(2.0 \times 10^{-3})(0.080)} = 0.75\ \text{Pa s}$ ✓

(c)
- weight − buoyancy $\propto r^3$ while drag $\propto rv$, so $v_t \propto r^2$ ✓
- $v_t = 0.080 \times 2^2 = 0.32\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

text:
A box is pulled $5.0\ \text{m}$ along horizontal ground by a rope. The tension in the rope is $40\ \text{N}$ and the rope makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. What is the work done by the tension?

A. $100\ \text{J}$
B. $173\ \text{J}$
C. $200\ \text{J}$
D. $0\ \text{J}$
ms: $W = Fs\cos\theta = 40 \times 5.0 \times \cos 60^\circ = 100\ \text{J}$. B uses $\sin 60^\circ$; C ignores the angle.

text:
A spring of spring constant $200\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ obeys Hooke's law. It is stretched from an extension of $0.10\ \text{m}$ to an extension of $0.20\ \text{m}$. What is the work done on the spring?

A. $1.0\ \text{J}$
B. $3.0\ \text{J}$
C. $4.0\ \text{J}$
D. $20\ \text{J}$
ms: $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2) = \frac{1}{2}(200)(0.040 - 0.010) = 3.0\ \text{J}$. A uses $\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2$; C is the total stored energy at 0.20 m; D is $k\Delta x$, a force, not an energy.

text:
An electric motor lifts a load of mass $50\ \text{kg}$ vertically through $12\ \text{m}$ at constant speed in $20\ \text{s}$. The electrical power input to the motor is $400\ \text{W}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. What is the efficiency of the motor?

A. $7.5\ \%$
B. $27\ \%$
C. $74\ \%$
D. $136\ \%$
ms: Useful power $= \frac{mgh}{t} = \frac{50 \times 9.8 \times 12}{20} = 294\ \text{W}$; efficiency $= \frac{294}{400} = 74\ \%$. A omits $g$; B is the fraction wasted; D inverts the ratio.

text:
A car travels at a constant speed of $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ along a level road. The total resistive force on the car is $600\ \text{N}$. What is the useful power output of the engine?

A. $20\ \text{W}$
B. $9.0\ \text{kW}$
C. $18\ \text{kW}$
D. $36\ \text{kW}$
ms: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so $P = Fv = 600 \times 30 = 1.8 \times 10^4\ \text{W}$. A divides instead of multiplying; B includes a spurious factor $\frac{1}{2}$.

text:
A block leaves a smooth slope with speed $v_0$ and slides onto a rough horizontal surface. The frictional force on the block is constant and the block comes to rest after sliding a distance $d$ on the rough surface. What is the speed of the block when it has slid a distance $\dfrac{d}{2}$?

A. $\dfrac{v_0}{2}$
B. $\dfrac{v_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
C. $\dfrac{v_0}{4}$
D. $v_0\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$
ms: Work done against friction is proportional to distance, so after $d/2$ half the initial kinetic energy has been dissipated: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2\right) \Rightarrow v = v_0/\sqrt{2}$. A assumes speed falls linearly with distance (it falls linearly with time).

text:
A student drops a ball of mass $0.058\ \text{kg}$ from rest from different heights $h_{\text{d}}$ onto a hard floor and records the height $h_{\text{r}}$ of the first rebound using a metre rule. The uncertainty in $h_{\text{r}}$ is $\pm 0.02\ \text{m}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

| $h_{\text{d}}$ / m | $h_{\text{r}}$ / m |
|---|---|
| 0.50 | 0.36 |
| 1.00 | 0.71 |
| 1.50 | 1.09 |
| 2.00 | 1.42 |

![graph of rebound height against drop height with straight line of best fit through the origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.3_6.svg)

(a) Calculate the percentage of the ball's initial gravitational potential energy that is dissipated in the bounce for $h_{\text{d}} = 1.00\ \text{m}$. [2]

(b) Determine the gradient of the graph and state what it represents physically. [2]

(c) Calculate the speed of the ball just after it leaves the floor when $h_{\text{d}} = 2.00\ \text{m}$. Ignore air resistance. [2]

(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $h_{\text{r}}$ for $h_{\text{d}} = 0.50\ \text{m}$, and suggest how the uncertainty in $h_{\text{r}}$ could be reduced. [2]
ms:
(a)
- energy retained fraction $= \frac{mgh_{\text{r}}}{mgh_{\text{d}}} = \frac{0.71}{1.00} = 0.71$ ✓
- percentage dissipated $= 29\ \%$ ✓

(b)
- gradient $\approx 0.71$ (accept 0.69–0.73) ✓
- the fraction of the energy (kinetic energy before impact) retained by the ball after the bounce / $\frac{E_{k}\ \text{after}}{E_{k}\ \text{before}}$ ✓

(c)
- $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh_{\text{r}}$ with $h_{\text{r}} = 1.42\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 1.42} = 5.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(d)
- $\frac{0.02}{0.36} \times 100 = 6\ \%$ (accept 5.6 %) ✓
- record the bounce on video (high frame rate) against a scale and read the maximum height frame by frame / view the top of the bounce at eye level to avoid parallax / repeat and average ✓

text:
A roller-coaster car of mass $500\ \text{kg}$ is released from rest at point P, at the top of a track $35\ \text{m}$ above the lowest point Q. It then climbs to the top of a second hill R, $20\ \text{m}$ above Q. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

![roller-coaster track: car at rest at P, 35 m above the lowest point Q; second hill R is 20 m above Q](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.3_7.svg)

(a) Assuming no energy is dissipated, calculate the speed of the car at Q. [2]

(b) Assuming no energy is dissipated, calculate the speed of the car at R. [2]

(c) The actual speed of the car at Q is $24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the energy dissipated between P and Q. [2]

(d) The length of track between P and Q is $80\ \text{m}$. Estimate the average resistive force on the car between P and Q. [1]

A car of mass $1200\ \text{kg}$ travels at a constant speed of $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ up a straight road inclined at $5.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. The total resistive force on the car is $450\ \text{N}$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the component of the car's weight acting parallel to the road. [1]

(b) Calculate the useful power output of the engine. [2]

(c) The overall efficiency of the engine is $30\ \%$. The fuel has an energy density of $3.4 \times 10^7\ \text{J}$ per litre (illustrative value). Determine the volume of fuel used when the car travels $1.0\ \text{km}$ up the road. [3]

(d) State one reason why the efficiency of the engine is less than $100\ \%$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $1200 \times 9.8 \times \sin 5.0^\circ = 1.0 \times 10^3\ \text{N}$ (1025 N) ✓

(b)
- driving force $= 1025 + 450 = 1475\ \text{N}$ ✓
- $P = Fv = 1475 \times 15 = 2.2 \times 10^4\ \text{W}$ ✓

(c)
- useful work over 1.0 km $= 1475 \times 1000 = 1.48 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$ (or $P \times 66.7\ \text{s}$) ✓
- energy input $= \frac{1.48 \times 10^6}{0.30} = 4.9 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$ ✓
- volume $= \frac{4.9 \times 10^6}{3.4 \times 10^7} = 0.14\ \text{litre}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- energy is dissipated as thermal energy in the engine/exhaust gases / friction between moving parts / sound ✓

text:
A toy launcher uses a spring of spring constant $800\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. The spring is compressed by $0.050\ \text{m}$ and then released, launching a ball of mass $0.020\ \text{kg}$ vertically upwards. Assume all the elastic potential energy is transferred to the kinetic energy of the ball, and measure heights from the point where the ball leaves the spring. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the compressed spring. [1]

(b) Ignoring air resistance, calculate the maximum height reached by the ball. [2]

(c) Ignoring air resistance, calculate the speed of the ball when it is $3.0\ \text{m}$ above the launch point. [2]

(d) In fact the ball reaches a maximum height of $4.6\ \text{m}$. Determine the average air resistance force on the ball during its ascent. [2]

(e) Explain, with reference to energy, why the ball returns to the launch point with a speed lower than its launch speed. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $E_p = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}(800)(0.050)^2 = 1.0\ \text{J}$ ✓

(b)
- $mgh = 1.0\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $h = \frac{1.0}{0.020 \times 9.8} = 5.1\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- $E_k = 1.0 - 0.020 \times 9.8 \times 3.0 = 0.41\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.41}{0.020}} = 6.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(d)
- energy dissipated $= 1.0 - 0.020 \times 9.8 \times 4.6 = 0.098\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $F = \frac{0.098}{4.6} = 0.021\ \text{N}$ ✓

(e)
- air resistance opposes the motion both on the way up and on the way down, so work is done against it throughout ✓
- some of the initial kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy of the air/ball, so the kinetic energy on return (with zero change in gravitational potential energy) is less ✓

text:
An object of mass $2.0\ \text{kg}$ is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force $F$ acts on the object in its direction of motion. The graph shows how $F$ varies with the displacement $x$ of the object.

![force-displacement graph: rises linearly from 0 to 8 N at 2 m, constant 8 N to 5 m, falls linearly to zero at 6 m](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.3_10.svg)

(a) Calculate the work done by $F$ as the object moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 6.0\ \text{m}$. [2]

(b) Calculate the speed of the object at $x = 6.0\ \text{m}$. [2]

(c) Determine the maximum power delivered to the object by $F$. [3]
ms:
(a)
- work = area under the graph: $\frac{1}{2}(2.0)(8.0) + (3.0)(8.0) + \frac{1}{2}(1.0)(8.0)$ ✓
- $= 8.0 + 24 + 4.0 = 36\ \text{J}$ ✓

(b)
- $\frac{1}{2}(2.0)v^2 = 36$ ✓
- $v = 6.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(c)
- $P = Fv$; between 2 m and 5 m $F$ is constant while $v$ increases, and beyond 5 m $F$ falls steeply while $v$ increases only slightly, so the maximum is at $x = 5.0\ \text{m}$ ✓
- work done up to 5.0 m $= 32\ \text{J}$ so $v = \sqrt{32} = 5.66\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
- $P_{\max} = 8.0 \times 5.66 = 45\ \text{W}$ ✓
- Award [2 max] for 48 W (using the final speed 6.0 m s⁻¹ with 8.0 N).

text:
A force of $20\ \text{N}$ is applied to the end of a spanner of length $0.30\ \text{m}$. The force acts at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the spanner. What is the torque of the force about the axis of the nut?

A. $3.0\ \text{N m}$
B. $5.2\ \text{N m}$
C. $6.0\ \text{N m}$
D. $67\ \text{N m}$
ms: $\tau = Fr\sin\theta = 20 \times 0.30 \times \sin 30^\circ = 3.0\ \text{N m}$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the spanner. B uses $\cos 30^\circ$; C ignores the angle; D divides $F$ by $r$.

text:
Four objects have the same mass $M$ and the same outer radius $R$. Which object has the greatest moment of inertia about an axis through its centre (for the cylinder and disc, the axis is perpendicular to the circular face)?

A. A solid sphere
B. A uniform solid disc
C. A thin ring
D. A uniform solid cylinder
ms: $I = \sum mr^2$: in a thin ring all the mass is at the maximum distance $R$ from the axis ($I = MR^2$), whereas the other objects have mass distributed closer to the axis ($\frac{2}{5}MR^2$, $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$, $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$).

text:
An ice skater spins at $2.0\ \text{rev s}^{-1}$ with her arms outstretched. Her moment of inertia is $4.0\ \text{kg m}^2$. She pulls her arms in, reducing her moment of inertia to $1.6\ \text{kg m}^2$. Friction is negligible. What happens to her rotational kinetic energy?

A. It is unchanged.
B. It increases by a factor of 2.5.
C. It increases by a factor of 6.25.
D. It decreases by a factor of 2.5.
ms: Angular momentum is conserved: $\omega$ increases by $\frac{4.0}{1.6} = 2.5$. $E_k = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}L\omega$, and $L$ is constant, so $E_k$ increases by 2.5 (the skater does work pulling her arms in). C squares the factor without allowing for the decrease in $I$; A wrongly assumes energy is conserved.

text:
A uniform horizontal beam of length $4.0\ \text{m}$ and weight $200\ \text{N}$ is hinged to a wall at one end. It is held horizontal by a vertical cable attached $3.0\ \text{m}$ from the hinge. A load of weight $100\ \text{N}$ hangs from the free end of the beam.

![horizontal beam hinged to a wall, vertical cable 3.0 m from the pivot, load hanging at the end 1.0 m further](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.4_4.svg)

What is the tension in the cable?

A. $133\ \text{N}$
B. $200\ \text{N}$
C. $267\ \text{N}$
D. $300\ \text{N}$
ms: Taking moments about the hinge: $T(3.0) = 200(2.0) + 100(4.0) = 800 \Rightarrow T = 267\ \text{N}$. D assumes the cable supports all the weight (it ignores the hinge force); A ignores the moment of the load; B is the beam's weight, not a result of taking moments.

text:
A flywheel with moment of inertia $0.50\ \text{kg m}^2$ rotates at $20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. A brake applies a constant frictional torque and the flywheel stops after completing exactly 40 revolutions. What is the magnitude of the frictional torque?

A. $0.40\ \text{N m}$
B. $0.80\ \text{N m}$
C. $2.5\ \text{N m}$
D. $5.0\ \text{N m}$
ms: $\theta = 40 \times 2\pi = 251\ \text{rad}$; $\omega^2 = 2\alpha\theta \Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{400}{2 \times 251} = 0.80\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$; $\tau = I\alpha = 0.50 \times 0.80 = 0.40\ \text{N m}$. B omits the 2 in $\omega^2 = 2\alpha\theta$; C uses 40 rad instead of 40 revolutions; D makes both mistakes.

text:
A student investigates the rotation of a flywheel mounted on a horizontal axle. A string wrapped around the axle (radius $0.025\ \text{m}$) supports a falling mass, which applies a torque $\tau$ to the flywheel. The angular acceleration $\alpha$ of the flywheel is measured with a light gate. A constant frictional torque $\tau_f$ acts at the axle. The uncertainty in $\alpha$ is $\pm 0.08\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$.

| $\tau$ / N m | $\alpha$ / rad s$^{-2}$ |
|---|---|
| 0.020 | 0.52 |
| 0.030 | 0.97 |
| 0.040 | 1.53 |
| 0.050 | 1.98 |
| 0.060 | 2.51 |

![graph of angular acceleration against applied torque; straight line with negative intercept on the alpha axis](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.4_6.svg)

(a) Explain why the graph is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. [2]

(b) Determine the moment of inertia of the flywheel. [2]

(c) Determine the frictional torque $\tau_f$. [1]

(d) The student calculated $\tau$ by assuming that the tension in the string equals the weight of the falling mass. Explain whether this assumption causes the values of $\tau$ to be overestimated or underestimated. [2]
ms:
(a)
- Newton's second law for rotation: $\tau - \tau_f = I\alpha$, so $\alpha = \frac{1}{I}\tau - \frac{\tau_f}{I}$, which is linear (gradient $\frac{1}{I}$) ✓
- the frictional torque must be overcome before there is any angular acceleration, so there is an intercept (on the $\tau$ axis at $\tau = \tau_f$; negative intercept on the $\alpha$ axis) ✓

(b)
- gradient $\approx 50\ \text{kg}^{-1}\ \text{m}^{-2}$ (accept 47–53) ✓
- $I = \frac{1}{\text{gradient}} = 0.020\ \text{kg m}^2$ ✓ (accept 0.019–0.021)

(c)
- $\tau_f$ = intercept on the $\tau$ axis $\approx 0.010\ \text{N m}$ (accept 0.008–0.012) ✓

(d)
- the mass accelerates downwards, so the tension is less than its weight: $T = m(g - a)$ ✓
- so the values of $\tau = Tr$ are overestimated (a systematic error) ✓

text:
A flywheel of moment of inertia $2.4\ \text{kg m}^2$ is initially at rest. A constant resultant torque of $6.0\ \text{N m}$ acts on it for $8.0\ \text{s}$.

(a) Calculate the angular acceleration of the flywheel. [1]

(b) Calculate the angular velocity of the flywheel after $8.0\ \text{s}$. [1]

(c) Calculate the number of revolutions the flywheel makes in the $8.0\ \text{s}$. [2]

(d) Calculate the rotational kinetic energy of the flywheel after $8.0\ \text{s}$. [1]

The torque is then removed. A disc of moment of inertia $1.6\ \text{kg m}^2$, initially not rotating, is dropped onto the same axle and quickly locks to the flywheel so they rotate together. Friction at the axle is negligible.

(e) Calculate the common angular velocity. [2]

(f) Determine the rotational kinetic energy lost when the disc locks to the flywheel and suggest what happens to this energy. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I} = \frac{6.0}{2.4} = 2.5\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$ ✓

(b)
- $\omega = \alpha t = 2.5 \times 8.0 = 20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓

(c)
- $\theta = \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2.5)(8.0)^2 = 80\ \text{rad}$ ✓
- $\frac{80}{2\pi} = 13$ revolutions (12.7) ✓

(d)
- $E_k = \frac{1}{2}(2.4)(20)^2 = 480\ \text{J}$ ✓

(e)
- conservation of angular momentum: $2.4 \times 20 = (2.4 + 1.6)\omega$ ✓
- $\omega = 12\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓

(f)
- final $E_k = \frac{1}{2}(4.0)(12)^2 = 288\ \text{J}$, so loss $= 480 - 288 = 192\ \text{J}$ ✓ (ECF from (d) and (e))
- transferred to thermal energy (and sound) by the friction between the disc and flywheel as they lock together ✓

text:
A uniform solid cylinder of mass $2.0\ \text{kg}$ and radius $0.10\ \text{m}$ is released from rest at the top of a slope of vertical height $1.5\ \text{m}$. It rolls down the slope without slipping. The moment of inertia of the cylinder about its axis is $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

![solid cylinder at the top of a slope of vertical height 1.5 m](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.4_8.svg)

(a) Show that the total kinetic energy of the cylinder when its centre moves with speed $v$ is $\frac{3}{4}Mv^2$. [2]

(b) Calculate the speed of the cylinder at the bottom of the slope. [2]

(c) State the fraction of the cylinder's kinetic energy that is rotational. [1]

(d) A thin hoop of the same mass and radius is released from rest at the top of an identical slope at the same time. It also rolls without slipping. Explain which object reaches the bottom first. [2]

(e) Friction acts on the cylinder at the point of contact. Explain why this friction is needed for rolling but does not reduce the total mechanical energy of the cylinder. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $E_k = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with $\omega = \frac{v}{R}$ ✓
- $= \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\frac{v^2}{R^2} = \frac{3}{4}Mv^2$ ✓

(b)
- $Mgh = \frac{3}{4}Mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{4gh}{3}}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 9.8 \times 1.5}{3}} = 4.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

(c)
- $\frac{1}{3}$ ✓

(d)
- the hoop has a larger moment of inertia ($MR^2$), so a larger fraction (one half) of its kinetic energy is rotational ✓
- so for the same loss of potential energy its translational speed at each point is smaller ($v = \sqrt{gh}$ at the bottom); the cylinder arrives first ✓

(e)
- friction at the contact point provides the torque about the centre that gives the angular acceleration (without it the cylinder would slide without rotating) ✓
- the contact point is instantaneously at rest (no slipping), so the static friction does no work / no energy is dissipated ✓

text:
A uniform ladder of length $5.0\ \text{m}$ and weight $150\ \text{N}$ rests with its top against a smooth vertical wall and its base on rough horizontal ground. The ladder makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground.

![ladder of length 5.0 m at 60 degrees to rough floor, leaning against a smooth wall](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.4_9.svg)

(a) State the two conditions for the ladder to be in equilibrium. [2]

(b) Show that the force exerted by the wall on the ladder is about $43\ \text{N}$. [3]

(c) Determine the minimum coefficient of static friction between the ladder and the ground. [2]

(d) A person starts to climb the ladder. State and explain how the frictional force needed at the base changes as the person climbs. [1]
ms:
(a)
- the resultant force on the ladder is zero ✓
- the resultant torque about any axis is zero ✓

(b)
- the wall force is horizontal (smooth wall); taking torques about the base ✓
- weight: $150 \times 2.5\cos 60^\circ = 187.5\ \text{N m}$; wall: $N_w \times 5.0\sin 60^\circ$ ✓
- $N_w = \frac{187.5}{4.33} = 43.3\ \text{N}$ ✓

(c)
- friction $= N_w = 43\ \text{N}$ and normal force from ground $= 150\ \text{N}$ ✓
- $\mu_s \geq \frac{43.3}{150} = 0.29$ ✓

(d)
- it increases, because the person's weight acts at a larger horizontal distance from the base as they climb, so a larger wall force (balanced by friction) is needed ✓

text:
A train moves east at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to the ground. A passenger walks towards the back of the train at $1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to the train. According to the Galilean transformation, what is the velocity of the passenger relative to the ground?

A. $21.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ east
B. $18.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ east
C. $18.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ west
D. $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ east
ms: $u = u' + v = -1.5 + 20 = 18.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, i.e. east. A adds the speeds as if the passenger walked forwards; C gets the direction wrong.

text:
Which are postulates of special relativity?

I. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames.
II. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers.
III. The time interval between two events is the same for all inertial observers.

A. I only
B. II only
C. I and II only
D. I, II and III
ms: Einstein's two postulates are I and II. Statement III is the Galilean assumption of absolute time, which special relativity rejects (time dilation follows from I and II).

text:
Muons have a mean lifetime of $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$ in their rest frame. A beam of muons moves at $0.98c$ relative to a laboratory. What is the mean lifetime of the muons measured in the laboratory?

A. $0.44\ \mu\text{s}$
B. $2.2\ \mu\text{s}$
C. $11\ \mu\text{s}$
D. $56\ \mu\text{s}$
ms: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.98^2}} = 5.0$; $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_0 = 5.0 \times 2.2 = 11\ \mu\text{s}$. A divides by $\gamma$ (confusing which time is proper); D multiplies by $\gamma^2$.

text:
A rod has a proper length of $4.0\ \text{m}$. It moves at $0.60c$ relative to an observer, parallel to its length. What length does the observer measure for the rod?

A. $2.4\ \text{m}$
B. $3.2\ \text{m}$
C. $4.0\ \text{m}$
D. $5.0\ \text{m}$
ms: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}} = 1.25$; $L = \frac{L_0}{\gamma} = \frac{4.0}{1.25} = 3.2\ \text{m}$. D multiplies by $\gamma$; A multiplies by $v/c$.

text:
Relative to the Earth, spaceship X moves at $0.80c$ to the east and spaceship Y moves at $0.60c$ to the west. What is the speed of Y relative to X?

A. $0.20c$
B. $0.38c$
C. $0.95c$
D. $1.4c$
ms: Taking east as positive, in the frame of X ($v = 0.80c$): $u' = \frac{u - v}{1 - uv/c^2} = \frac{-0.60c - 0.80c}{1 + 0.48} = -0.95c$, so the speed is $0.95c$. D is the Galilean result (exceeds $c$); A subtracts the speeds; B uses wrong signs in both numerator and denominator.

text:
Muons are produced high in the atmosphere and travel vertically downwards at $0.994c$. In its rest frame a muon has a half-life of $1.52\ \mu\text{s}$. A detector measures the count rate $R$ of muons at several altitudes $h$ above sea level (illustrative data). Assume all detected muons were produced above the highest altitude and travel at the same speed. Take $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

| $h$ / m | $R$ / min$^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| 0 | 100 |
| 500 | 109 |
| 1000 | 117 |
| 1500 | 129 |
| 2000 | 139 |

(a) Calculate the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ for the muons. [1]

(b) Calculate, in the Earth frame, the distance travelled by the muons in one half-life. [2]

The graph shows $\ln(R/\text{min}^{-1})$ plotted against $h$.

![graph of ln R against altitude h: straight line with positive gradient](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.5_6.svg)

(c) The count rate halves for each distance $L$ that the muons travel downwards, so the gradient of the graph is $\frac{\ln 2}{L}$. Determine $L$ from the graph and comment on your answer with reference to (b). [3]

(d) Explain how these data provide evidence for time dilation. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.994^2}} = 9.1$ ✓

(b)
- half-life in Earth frame $= 9.14 \times 1.52 = 13.9\ \mu\text{s}$ ✓
- distance $= 0.994 \times 3.00 \times 10^8 \times 13.9 \times 10^{-6} = 4.1 \times 10^3\ \text{m}$ ✓
- Alternative: in the muon frame the atmosphere is contracted; same result.

(c)
- gradient from the line, e.g. $\frac{4.936 - 4.605}{2000} \approx 1.65 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{-1}$ (accept 1.5 to 1.8 $\times 10^{-4}$) ✓
- $L = \frac{\ln 2}{\text{gradient}} \approx 4.2 \times 10^3\ \text{m}$ ✓ (accept 3.9 to 4.6 km)
- agrees (to within experimental uncertainty) with the distance calculated using the dilated half-life in (b) ✓

(d)
- without time dilation the muons would travel only $0.994c \times 1.52\ \mu\text{s} = 453\ \text{m}$ per half-life ✓
- the rate would then increase by a factor of about $2^{2000/453} \approx 20$ over 2000 m, whereas only a factor of about 1.4 is observed / far more muons survive to sea level than predicted without time dilation ✓

text:
Reference frame S′ moves at $0.60c$ relative to reference frame S in the positive $x$-direction. The origins coincide at $t = t' = 0$. An event E has coordinates $x = 900\ \text{m}$, $t = 2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ in frame S. Take $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Calculate the position $x'$ of event E in frame S′. [2]

(b) Calculate the time $t'$ of event E in frame S′. [2]

(c) Show that the spacetime interval between event E and the event at the origin ($x = 0$, $t = 0$) is the same in both frames. [2]

(d) Deduce whether the event at the origin could have caused event E. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\gamma = 1.25$ and $x' = \gamma(x - vt) = 1.25(900 - 0.60 \times 3.00 \times 10^8 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6})$ ✓
- $x' = 1.25(900 - 360) = 675\ \text{m}$ ✓

(b)
- $t' = \gamma\left(t - \frac{vx}{c^2}\right) = 1.25\left(2.0 \times 10^{-6} - \frac{0.60 \times 900}{3.00 \times 10^8}\right)$ ✓
- $t' = 1.25(2.0 - 1.8) \times 10^{-6} = 0.25\ \mu\text{s}$ ✓

(c)
- in S: $(ct)^2 - x^2 = 600^2 - 900^2 = -4.5 \times 10^5\ \text{m}^2$ ✓
- in S′: $(ct')^2 - x'^2 = 75^2 - 675^2 = -4.5 \times 10^5\ \text{m}^2$, the same ✓
- Accept the opposite sign convention used consistently. Allow ECF from (a) and (b).

(d)
- the interval is space-like: $x > ct$ ($900\ \text{m} > 600\ \text{m}$), so light could not travel from the origin to E in the time available ✓
- so no causal link is possible; E cannot have been caused by the event at the origin ✓

text:
The spacetime diagram shows the axes of frame S (an Earth observer) and the axes $ct'$ and $x'$ of frame S′ (a spacecraft) moving at constant velocity relative to S. The origins coincide. Distances are in light-years (ly). Events A, B and P are marked.

![spacetime diagram with x and ct axes, ct-prime axis through (1, 2), x-prime axis, light line at 45 degrees and events A (1, 1.5), B (3, 2.5), P (1, 2)](qbank/img/gen_phys_A.5_8.svg)

(a) Show that the speed of S′ relative to S is $0.50c$. [2]

(b) Show that events A and B are simultaneous in frame S′. [2]

(c) State, according to frame S, which of the events A and B happens first, and the time interval between them. [1]

(d) Event P is on the $ct'$ axis. Determine the time of event P measured in frame S′. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the $ct'$ axis is the worldline of the origin of S′; it passes through $x = 1.0\ \text{ly}$, $ct = 2.0\ \text{ly}$ ✓
- $\frac{v}{c} = \frac{x}{ct} = \frac{1.0}{2.0} = 0.50$ ✓
- Accept $\tan\theta = 0.50$ using the angle between the $ct'$ and $ct$ axes.

(b)
- the line AB has gradient $\frac{\Delta(ct)}{\Delta x} = \frac{2.5 - 1.5}{3.0 - 1.0} = 0.50$, the same as the $x'$ axis ✓
- so AB is parallel to the $x'$ axis, i.e. a line of constant $t'$: A and B are simultaneous in S′ ✓

(c)
- A happens first; B occurs 1.0 year later ✓

(d)
- P lies on the worldline of the S′ origin, so $t'$ is a proper time: $(ct')^2 = (ct)^2 - x^2 = 2.0^2 - 1.0^2$ ✓
- $ct' = 1.7\ \text{ly}$ so $t' = 1.7\ \text{years}$ ✓
- Alternative: $\gamma = 1.15$, $t' = \frac{2.0}{1.15} = 1.7\ \text{years}$.

text:
A spacecraft leaves Earth and travels at a constant $0.80c$ to a star that is $12\ \text{ly}$ from Earth, as measured in the Earth frame. Ignore the periods of acceleration.

(a) Calculate the time taken for the journey in the Earth frame. [1]

(b) Calculate the time taken for the journey as measured by a clock on the spacecraft. [2]

(c) Calculate the distance from Earth to the star in the spacecraft frame and show that it is consistent with your answer to (b). [2]

(d) On arrival at the star, the spacecraft sends a radio signal to Earth. Determine how long after the departure of the spacecraft, in the Earth frame, the signal is received on Earth. [1]

(e) As it approaches the star, the spacecraft launches a probe forwards at $0.50c$ relative to the spacecraft. Calculate the speed of the probe relative to Earth. [2]

(f) The spacecraft then returns to Earth at the same speed. On return, the crew have aged less than people on Earth. Explain why this is not a contradiction even though, during each leg of the journey, each observer sees the other's clock running slow. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $t = \frac{12}{0.80} = 15\ \text{years}$ ✓

(b)
- $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.64}} = \frac{5}{3}$ (1.67) ✓
- $t_0 = \frac{15}{1.67} = 9.0\ \text{years}$ ✓

(c)
- $L = \frac{12}{1.67} = 7.2\ \text{ly}$ ✓
- time $= \frac{7.2}{0.80} = 9.0\ \text{years}$, the same as (b) ✓

(d)
- $15 + 12 = 27\ \text{years}$ ✓

(e)
- $u = \frac{0.80c + 0.50c}{1 + 0.80 \times 0.50}$ ✓
- $u = 0.93c$ ✓

(f)
- the situation is not symmetric: the spacecraft changes inertial frame (decelerates/turns round), while the Earth stays in one inertial frame ✓
- so only the Earth observer's analysis in a single inertial frame applies throughout; on a spacetime diagram the spacecraft's worldline between the same two events (departure and return) has a shorter proper time ✓

text:
A solid sample is heated by a heater of constant power. All the energy supplied is absorbed by the sample. The graph shows how the temperature of the sample varies with time.

![Temperature against time: rises from -40 °C to 0 °C in 2 min, constant at 0 °C until 10 min, then rises to 60 °C at 16 min](qbank/img/gen_phys_B.1_1.svg)

What is $\dfrac{\text{specific heat capacity of the liquid}}{\text{specific heat capacity of the solid}}$?

A. 0.50
B. 1.0
C. 2.0
D. 4.0
ms: **C.** With constant power $P$, $P = mc\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$, so $c \propto \dfrac{1}{\text{gradient}}$. Solid: $40\ \text{K}$ in 2 min $= 20\ \text{K min}^{-1}$; liquid: $60\ \text{K}$ in 6 min $= 10\ \text{K min}^{-1}$. The liquid warms at half the rate, so its specific heat capacity is twice as large. A comes from taking $c$ proportional to the gradient instead of inversely proportional.

text:
Two cylindrical rods, X and Y, are made of the same material. Rod Y has twice the length and twice the diameter of rod X. The sides of both rods are insulated and the ends of each rod are kept at the same two temperatures.

What is $\dfrac{\text{rate of thermal energy transfer through Y}}{\text{rate of thermal energy transfer through X}}$?

A. 0.5
B. 1
C. 2
D. 4
ms: **C.** $\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = kA\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$. Doubling the diameter multiplies $A$ by 4; doubling the length halves the temperature gradient. Ratio $= 4 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 2$. D ignores the length; B treats the area as proportional to the diameter.

text:
Two stars, X and Y, have the same radius. The spectrum of X has its peak intensity at a wavelength of 400 nm and the spectrum of Y has its peak at 800 nm. Both stars may be treated as black bodies.

What is $\dfrac{\text{luminosity of X}}{\text{luminosity of Y}}$?

A. $\dfrac{1}{16}$
B. 2
C. 4
D. 16
ms: **D.** By Wien's law $T \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\max}}$, so $T_X = 2T_Y$. With equal radii $L = \sigma 4\pi R^2 T^4 \propto T^4$, giving $2^4 = 16$. A inverts the ratio (treats $L \propto \lambda_{\max}^4$); B uses $L \propto T$.

text:
Two stars, P and Q, have the same apparent brightness when viewed from Earth. The surface temperature of P is twice that of Q, and P is four times as far from Earth as Q.

What is $\dfrac{\text{radius of P}}{\text{radius of Q}}$?

A. $\dfrac{1}{4}$
B. 1
C. 2
D. 4
ms: **B.** $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2} = \dfrac{\sigma 4\pi R^2 T^4}{4\pi d^2} \propto \dfrac{R^2T^4}{d^2}$. Equal $b$: $R_P^2 \times 2^4 / 4^2 = R_Q^2$, so $R_P = R_Q$. A ignores the distance; D ignores the temperature.

text:
Which statements about a black body are correct?


I. It absorbs all the electromagnetic radiation incident on it.

II. Its emissivity is 1.

III. The wavelength at which its emitted intensity is a maximum increases as its temperature increases.

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** A black body is a perfect absorber and perfect emitter, so its emissivity is 1. By Wien's displacement law $\lambda_{\max}T = 2.9\times10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$, so the peak wavelength *decreases* as temperature increases; III is false.

text:
A student determines the specific latent heat of vaporization $L_v$ of water. An electric kettle containing water stands on a top-pan balance. The heating element has a constant power output of 1800 W. Once the water is boiling steadily, the student records the balance reading at regular intervals.

| time $t$ / s | 0 | 60 | 120 | 180 | 240 | 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mass $m$ / g | 812 | 765 | 719 | 671 | 625 | 578 |

(a) Suggest why the readings are taken only once the water is boiling steadily. [1]

(b) Determine the rate at which water is converted to steam, in $\text{kg s}^{-1}$. [2]

(c) Determine, using your answer to (b), a value for $L_v$. [2]

(d) The accepted value of $L_v$ is $2.26\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. Explain whether thermal energy losses to the surroundings can account for the difference between the accepted value and your value in (c). [2]

(e) The student repeats the experiment with the power output set to 1200 W and finds that the rate of mass loss is $0.515\ \text{g s}^{-1}$. Assuming that the rate of thermal energy loss to the surroundings is the same in both experiments, determine $L_v$. [3]
ms:
**(a)**
- so that all the energy supplied goes into changing state / none is used to raise the temperature of the water ✓

**(b)**
- gradient using widely separated values, e.g. $\dfrac{812 - 578}{300}$ ✓
- $7.8\times10^{-4}\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept $7.7$–$7.9\times10^{-4}\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$. Award [1 max] for an answer left in $\text{g s}^{-1}$ (0.78).

**(c)**
- $P = L_v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$ so $L_v = \dfrac{1800}{7.8\times10^{-4}}$ ✓
- $2.3\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- with losses, less than 1800 W is used to vaporize the water, so the rate of mass loss is smaller than it would be without losses ✓
- so $L_v = P/\text{rate}$ is an overestimate; the experimental value is larger than the accepted value, so the losses can account for the difference ✓

**(e)**
- $1800 = L_v(7.8\times10^{-4}) + h$ AND $1200 = L_v(5.15\times10^{-4}) + h$, where $h$ is the rate of energy loss ✓
- subtracting: $600 = L_v(2.65\times10^{-4})$ ✓
- $L_v = 2.26\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept $2.2$–$2.3\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ (ECF from (b)). Rate of loss $h \approx 34\ \text{W}$ is not required.

text:
The graph shows the spectrum of the radiation emitted by a star. The star may be treated as a black body.

![Black-body spectrum: intensity against wavelength from 0 to 3000 nm, single peak](qbank/img/gen_phys_B.1_7.svg)

(a) Determine the surface temperature of the star. [2]

(b) The radius of the star is $2.0\times10^{9}\ \text{m}$. Show that the luminosity of the star is about $7\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$. [2]

(c) The apparent brightness of the star measured at Earth is $3.2\times10^{-9}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Calculate the distance from Earth to the star. [2]

(d) A second star has the same radius as this star but a higher surface temperature. Describe how its spectrum would differ from the one shown. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- peak wavelength read as 725 nm ✓ (accept 700–750 nm)
- $T = \dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{725\times10^{-9}} = 4.0\times10^{3}\ \text{K}$ ✓

Accept 3900–4100 K consistent with the reading.

**(b)**
- $L = \sigma 4\pi R^2T^4 = 5.67\times10^{-8} \times 4\pi \times (2.0\times10^{9})^2 \times (4.0\times10^{3})^4$ ✓
- $= 7.3\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$ ✓

Answer to at least 2 s.f. required for the "show that".

**(c)**
- $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{4\pi b}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7.3\times10^{26}}{4\pi \times 3.2\times10^{-9}}}$ ✓
- $1.3\times10^{17}\ \text{m}$ ✓

Use of $7\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$ gives $1.3\times10^{17}\ \text{m}$; also accept.

**(d)**
- peak at a shorter wavelength ✓
- intensity greater at every wavelength / total area under the curve greater (since $L \propto T^4$) ✓

text:
A drink consists of 0.25 kg of water at 30 °C in an insulated cup of negligible heat capacity. An ice cube of mass 0.040 kg at a temperature of −18 °C is added to the drink.

- Specific heat capacity of water $= 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$
- Specific heat capacity of ice $= 2100\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$
- Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.34\times10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$

(a) Distinguish between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat of fusion. [2]

(b) Show that the energy required to warm the ice to 0 °C and melt it completely is about $1.5\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$. [2]

(c) Determine the final temperature of the drink. [3]

(d) Explain, with reference to the molecules, why the temperature of the ice does not change while it is melting. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- specific heat capacity: energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass by 1 K ✓
- specific latent heat of fusion: energy required to change unit mass from solid to liquid at constant temperature ✓

**(b)**
- warming: $0.040 \times 2100 \times 18 = 1.5\times10^{3}\ \text{J}$ AND melting: $0.040 \times 3.34\times10^{5} = 1.34\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- total $= 1.49\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$ ✓

**(c)**
- energy lost by warm water $= 0.25 \times 4200 \times (30 - T)$ ✓
- $0.25 \times 4200 \times (30 - T) = 1.49\times10^{4} + 0.040 \times 4200 \times T$ ✓
- $T = 14\ \text{°C}$ ✓

Accept 13.6–13.7 °C. Award [2 max] if the melted ice is not warmed from 0 °C to $T$ (gives 15.8 °C).

**(d)**
- energy supplied is used to increase the (intermolecular) potential energy of the molecules / break bonds between molecules ✓
- the mean kinetic energy of the molecules does not change, and temperature is a measure of mean kinetic energy ✓

text:
(a) Outline how thermal energy is conducted through a non-metallic solid such as glass. [2]

(b) A single pane of glass has an area of $1.5\ \text{m}^2$ and a thickness of 4.0 mm. The thermal conductivity of the glass is $0.80\ \text{W m}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. The inner surface of the glass is at 10.0 °C and the outer surface is at 6.0 °C. Calculate the rate of thermal energy transfer through the glass. [2]

(c) A double-glazed window unit of area $1.5\ \text{m}^2$ consists of two panes of the same glass, each 4.0 mm thick, separated by a 12 mm layer of still air. The thermal conductivity of still air is $0.025\ \text{W m}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. The inner surface of the unit is at 18.0 °C and the outer surface is at 4.0 °C.

![Cross-section of a double-glazed unit: 4.0 mm glass, 12 mm still air, 4.0 mm glass; inside 18.0 °C, outside 4.0 °C](qbank/img/gen_phys_B.1_9.svg)

(i) State why, when conditions are steady, the rate of thermal energy transfer is the same through each of the three layers. [1]

(ii) Determine the rate of thermal energy transfer through the unit. [3]

(iii) Hence calculate the temperature difference across the air layer. [1]

(d) Suggest why the air gap in the unit should not be made very much wider. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- particles/atoms at the hotter end vibrate with greater amplitude/kinetic energy ✓
- and pass energy to neighbouring particles through collisions/bonds (lattice vibrations), so energy moves towards the cooler end ✓

**(b)**
- $\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = kA\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x} = 0.80 \times 1.5 \times \dfrac{4.0}{4.0\times10^{-3}}$ ✓
- $1.2\times10^{3}\ \text{W}$ ✓

**(c)(i)**
- temperatures are not changing, so no energy accumulates in any layer: energy entering a layer per second equals energy leaving it ✓

**(c)(ii)**
- for each layer $\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta x}{kA}$ (same rate $P$ through each) ✓
- $14.0 = P\left(2\times\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-3}}{0.80\times1.5} + \dfrac{12\times10^{-3}}{0.025\times1.5}\right) = P(6.67\times10^{-3} + 0.320)$ ✓
- $P = 43\ \text{W}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for treating the unit as 12 mm of air only (44 W) without justification; award [0] for adding conductivities.

**(c)(iii)**
- $\Delta T_{\text{air}} = 43 \times 0.320 = 13.7\ \text{K}$ ✓ (accept 14 K; ECF from (c)(ii))

**(d)**
- in a wide gap convection currents can be set up in the air, increasing the rate of energy transfer ✓

text:
The skin of a person has a surface area of $1.8\ \text{m}^2$ and a temperature of 33 °C. The emissivity of skin is 0.97.

(a) State what is meant by emissivity. [1]

(b) Calculate the power radiated by the skin. [2]

(c) The person is in a room whose walls are at 20 °C. Assume the skin absorbs radiation from the room with the same emissivity. Calculate the net rate of energy loss from the skin by radiation. [2]

(d) Calculate the wavelength at which the radiation emitted by the skin has maximum intensity, and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which it lies. [2]

(e) Explain why a person wearing clothes loses thermal energy at a lower rate than an unclothed person in the same room. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- the ratio of the power radiated by the surface to the power radiated by a black body of the same area and temperature ✓

**(b)**
- $P = e\sigma AT^4 = 0.97 \times 5.67\times10^{-8} \times 1.8 \times 306^4$ ✓
- $870\ \text{W}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for use of 33 K.

**(c)**
- $P_{\text{net}} = e\sigma A(306^4 - 293^4)$ ✓
- $140\ \text{W}$ ✓ (accept 138 W)

**(d)**
- $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{306} = 9.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$ ✓
- infrared ✓

**(e)**
- the outer surface of the clothes is at a lower temperature than the skin, so it radiates less power ($\propto T^4$) ✓
- air trapped in the fabric is a poor conductor and cannot circulate, reducing conduction and convection ✓

text:
Averaged over Earth's surface, the intensity of solar radiation incident on the top of the atmosphere is $340\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. An intensity of $102\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ is reflected or scattered back into space.

What is the albedo of Earth?

A. 0.30
B. 0.43
C. 0.70
D. 3.3
ms: **A.** Albedo $= \dfrac{\text{scattered power}}{\text{incident power}} = \dfrac{102}{340} = 0.30$. C is the fraction absorbed; B divides by the absorbed intensity (238); D is the inverse.

text:
The solar constant is $S$. Why is the mean intensity of solar radiation incident on the top of Earth's atmosphere, averaged over the whole of Earth's surface, equal to $\dfrac{S}{4}$?

A. About three-quarters of the incident radiation is reflected by clouds.
B. The surface area of Earth is four times the area of the disc that intercepts the radiation.
C. At any time, half of Earth is in darkness.
D. The intensity falls with the square of the distance between the Sun and Earth.
ms: **B.** Earth intercepts power $S\pi R^2$, which is spread over a total surface area $4\pi R^2$, giving $S/4$. A confuses this with albedo (about 0.3); C accounts for a factor of only 2 (it ignores the oblique incidence on the sunlit hemisphere); D explains how $S$ depends on distance, not the factor of 4.

text:
Which statement explains why carbon dioxide and water vapour are greenhouse gases?

A. They absorb most of the visible radiation from the Sun before it reaches the surface.
B. They reflect infrared radiation emitted by the surface back towards the ground.
C. They destroy ozone, allowing more ultraviolet radiation to reach the surface.
D. Their molecules have natural frequencies of vibration in the infrared region, so they absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-emit it in all directions.
ms: **D.** Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming visible radiation but absorb the infrared emitted by the surface because the radiation frequency matches the natural (resonant) frequencies of molecular vibration; re-emission in all directions returns some energy to the surface. B is a common misconception (absorption and re-emission, not reflection); A and C are incorrect mechanisms.

text:
A planet with no atmosphere has an albedo of 0.30 and a mean equilibrium surface temperature $T$. The planet behaves as a black-body emitter. The albedo increases to 0.40 while the incident solar intensity is unchanged.

What is the new mean equilibrium surface temperature?

A. $0.86T$
B. $0.93T$
C. $0.96T$
D. $1.04T$
ms: **C.** At equilibrium $(1-\alpha)\dfrac{S}{4} = \sigma T^4$, so $T \propto (1-\alpha)^{1/4}$: $T_{\text{new}} = T\left(\dfrac{0.60}{0.70}\right)^{1/4} = 0.96T$. A omits the fourth root and B uses a square root; D has the temperature rising, though more radiation is reflected.

text:
A simple model of a planet with no atmosphere uses the following illustrative data for its surface.

| surface type | fraction of total surface area | albedo |
|---|---|---|
| ocean | 0.70 | 0.06 |
| land | 0.20 | 0.15 |
| ice | 0.10 | 0.80 |

The solar constant at the planet is $1.36\times10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. The planet emits as a black body.

(a) Define albedo. [1]

(b) Show that the mean albedo of the planet is about 0.15. [2]

(c) Determine the mean equilibrium surface temperature predicted by the model. [2]

(d) In a warmer climate the fraction covered by ice falls to 0.05 and the uncovered area becomes ocean. Determine the change in the mean equilibrium surface temperature. [2]

(e) Explain why the melting of ice is described as a positive feedback mechanism. [2]

(f) The ice is found mainly near the poles. Suggest why the model therefore overestimates the effect of the ice on the planet's energy balance. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- ratio of the (total) scattered/reflected power to the (total) incident power ✓

**(b)**
- weighted mean: $0.70 \times 0.06 + 0.20 \times 0.15 + 0.10 \times 0.80$ ✓
- $= 0.042 + 0.030 + 0.080 = 0.152$ ✓

**(c)**
- $\sigma T^4 = (1-\alpha)\dfrac{S}{4} = 0.848 \times \dfrac{1360}{4} = 288\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓
- $T = 267\ \text{K}$ ✓

Accept 266–268 K. Award [1 max] if the factor of 4 is omitted (378 K).

**(d)**
- new albedo $= 0.75 \times 0.06 + 0.030 + 0.05 \times 0.80 = 0.115$ AND new $T = 270\ \text{K}$ ✓
- increase of about 3 K ✓

Accept 2.8–3.0 K; ECF from (c).

**(e)**
- higher temperature melts ice, replacing a high-albedo surface with a low-albedo one ✓
- so more radiation is absorbed, increasing the temperature further (the effect amplifies the original change) ✓

**(f)**
- near the poles the radiation arrives at a low angle / the incident intensity per unit area is smaller, so the ice reflects less power than its area fraction implies ✓

text:
(a) Describe the greenhouse effect. [3]

(b) The mean surface temperature of Earth is 288 K. Calculate the intensity of the radiation emitted by the surface, assuming it behaves as a black body. [1]

(c) The mean intensity of the radiation leaving the top of Earth's atmosphere is $240\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Calculate the effective emissivity of Earth (surface and atmosphere) as seen from space. [2]

(d) Suggest how the value in (c) would change if the concentration of greenhouse gases increased while the surface temperature remained at 288 K. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the surface ✓
- the surface emits longer-wavelength (infrared) radiation, which is absorbed by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere ✓
- the gases re-emit infrared in all directions, some back towards the surface, so the surface is warmer than it would be without the atmosphere ✓

**(b)**
- $\sigma T^4 = 5.67\times10^{-8} \times 288^4 = 390\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $e = \dfrac{240}{390}$ ✓
- $0.62$ ✓ (accept 0.61–0.62; ECF from (b))

**(d)**
- it would decrease, because more of the surface radiation is absorbed and less escapes to space ✓

text:
The diagram shows a simple energy balance model of a planet. The mean intensity of solar radiation incident on the top of the atmosphere is $340\ \text{W m}^{-2}$, and 30 % of it is reflected back into space. The atmosphere is transparent to solar radiation. The surface behaves as a black body. In the first version of the model, the atmosphere absorbs all of the infrared radiation emitted by the surface and emits an intensity $I_a$ both upwards and downwards.

![Energy balance model: solar radiation passes through the atmosphere to the surface; the surface emits sigma Ts^4 up to the atmosphere; the atmosphere emits Ia upwards to space and Ia downwards to the surface](qbank/img/gen_phys_B.2_7.svg)

(a) Show that the intensity of solar radiation absorbed by the surface is about $240\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. [1]

(b) By considering the energy balance of the planet as a whole, state the value of $I_a$. [1]

(c) Determine the surface temperature $T_s$. [3]

(d) Determine the temperature $T_a$ of the atmosphere, assuming it radiates as a black body. [1]

(e) The actual mean surface temperature is 288 K. In an improved model, the atmosphere absorbs only a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the infrared radiation from the surface, the rest passing directly into space, and emits an intensity $\varepsilon\sigma T_a^4$ in each direction. Determine $\varepsilon$. [3]
ms:
**(a)**
- $0.70 \times 340 = 238\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓

**(b)**
- only $I_a$ leaves the planet as infrared, so $I_a = 238\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓

**(c)**
- energy balance at the surface: $238 + I_a = \sigma T_s^4$ ✓
- $\sigma T_s^4 = 476\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓
- $T_s = 303\ \text{K}$ ✓

**(d)**
- $T_a = \left(\dfrac{238}{5.67\times10^{-8}}\right)^{1/4} = 255\ \text{K}$ ✓

**(e)**
- atmosphere: $\varepsilon\sigma T_s^4 = 2\varepsilon\sigma T_a^4$, so $\sigma T_a^4 = \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma T_s^4$ ✓
- top of atmosphere: $(1-\varepsilon)\sigma T_s^4 + \varepsilon\sigma T_a^4 = 238$, so $\sigma T_s^4\left(1 - \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\right) = 238$ ✓
- $\sigma T_s^4 = 390\ \text{W m}^{-2}$, giving $1 - \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2} = 0.61$ and $\varepsilon = 0.78$ ✓

Alternative: surface balance $238 + \varepsilon\sigma T_a^4 = \sigma T_s^4$ leads to the same result. Accept 0.77–0.79.

text:
The luminosity of the Sun is $3.83\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$.

(a) The mean distance from the Sun to Earth is $1.50\times10^{11}\ \text{m}$. Show that the solar constant at Earth is about $1.35\times10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. [1]

(b) The mean distance from the Sun to Mars is $2.28\times10^{11}\ \text{m}$. Calculate the intensity of solar radiation at the distance of Mars. [1]

(c) Explain why the mean intensity of solar radiation incident per unit area of the surface of Mars is one-quarter of your answer to (b). [2]

(d) The albedo of Mars is 0.25. Determine the mean equilibrium surface temperature of Mars, assuming that it behaves as a black body and has no atmosphere. [2]

(e) The measured mean surface temperature of Mars is close to the value in (d). Suggest what this indicates about the atmosphere of Mars. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\dfrac{3.83\times10^{26}}{4\pi(1.50\times10^{11})^2} = 1.35\times10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓ (answer to at least 3 s.f.: 1355)

**(b)**
- $\dfrac{3.83\times10^{26}}{4\pi(2.28\times10^{11})^2} = 586\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓ (accept 590)

**(c)**
- the radiation is intercepted by the cross-sectional area $\pi R^2$ ✓
- but is spread (as the planet rotates) over the whole surface area $4\pi R^2$ ✓

**(d)**
- $\sigma T^4 = 0.75 \times \dfrac{586}{4} = 110\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ ✓
- $T = 210\ \text{K}$ ✓ (ECF from (b))

**(e)**
- the atmosphere is very thin / has little greenhouse effect ✓

text:
The pressure of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is doubled and its volume is halved.

What happens to the absolute temperature of the gas?

A. It is quartered.
B. It is halved.
C. It is unchanged.
D. It is doubled.
ms: **C.** $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ is constant for a fixed mass; $pV$ is unchanged ($2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 1$), so $T$ is unchanged.

text:
Which is **not** an assumption of the kinetic model of an ideal gas?

A. Collisions between molecules are elastic.
B. The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
C. There are no intermolecular forces except during collisions.
D. All the molecules move with the same speed.
ms: **D.** The molecules have a distribution of speeds (only the mean kinetic energy is fixed by temperature). A, B and C are all assumptions of the model.

text:
The temperature of an ideal gas increases from 27 °C to 327 °C.

What is $\dfrac{\text{new root mean square speed of the molecules}}{\text{original root mean square speed of the molecules}}$?

A. 1.4
B. 2.0
C. 3.5
D. 12
ms: **A.** $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{rms}}^2 = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$, so $v_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T}$ with $T$ in kelvin: $\sqrt{600/300} = \sqrt{2} = 1.4$. B forgets the square root; C and D use Celsius temperatures.

text:
Container X has volume $V$ and holds $n$ moles of an ideal gas at temperature $T$. Container Y has volume $2V$ and holds the same ideal gas at temperature $2T$. The pressure in both containers is the same.

What is the amount of gas in container Y?

A. $\dfrac{n}{2}$
B. $n$
C. $2n$
D. $4n$
ms: **B.** $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT}$; for Y, $\dfrac{p(2V)}{R(2T)} = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = n$. D multiplies both factors; A and C account for only one of them.

text:
A sealed container holds a mixture of helium (molar mass $4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) and neon (molar mass $20\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) in thermal equilibrium. Both behave as ideal gases.


I. The mean kinetic energy of the helium atoms equals the mean kinetic energy of the neon atoms.

II. The root mean square speed of the helium atoms is $\sqrt{5}$ times that of the neon atoms.

III. The pressure exerted by the helium equals the pressure exerted by the neon.

Which statements are correct?

A. I only
B. II only
C. I and II only
D. I, II and III
ms: **C.** Both gases are at the same temperature, so $\bar{E}_k = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$ is the same (I). Then $v_{\text{rms}} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$, giving $\sqrt{20/4} = \sqrt{5}$ (II). The pressure of each gas depends on the number of atoms of that gas, which is not given, so III need not be true.

text:
A student investigates the relationship between the pressure $p$ and volume of a fixed mass of air at constant temperature. The air is trapped in a syringe connected by a tube to a pressure gauge. The student records the volume $V$ read from the syringe scale and the pressure $p$.

| $V$ / $\text{cm}^3$ | 22.0 | 18.0 | 14.0 | 10.0 | 6.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p$ / kPa | 100 | 120 | 150 | 200 | 300 |

(a) State one quantity, other than temperature, that must be kept constant in this experiment. [1]

(b) Show that the data do **not** support the hypothesis that $pV$ is constant. [2]

(c) The student suggests that the air in the connecting tube, of volume $V_0$, was not included in the readings. The graph shows $V$ plotted against $\dfrac{1}{p}$.

![Graph of V in cm^3 against 1/p in 10^-3 kPa^-1 with five data points and a straight best-fit line extended to the vertical axis](qbank/img/gen_phys_B.3_6.svg)

(i) Use the graph to determine $V_0$. [2]

(ii) Determine the gradient of the line and state what it represents. [2]

(d) The temperature of the air was 20 °C. Determine the amount, in mol, of air trapped in the apparatus. [2]

(e) Suggest why the student pushed the plunger in slowly. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- the mass/amount of gas (no leaks) ✓

**(b)**
- calculates $pV$ for at least two readings, e.g. $100 \times 22.0 = 2200$ and $300 \times 6.0 = 1800\ \text{kPa cm}^3$ ✓
- the values differ by far more than the experimental uncertainty / decrease steadily, so $pV$ is not constant ✓

**(c)(i)**
- $p(V + V_0) = \text{constant}$, so $V = \dfrac{\text{constant}}{p} - V_0$ and the vertical intercept is $-V_0$ ✓
- $V_0 = 2.0\ \text{cm}^3$ ✓ (accept 1.8–2.2)

**(c)(ii)**
- gradient $= \dfrac{22.0 - (-2.0)}{10\times10^{-3}} = 2.4\times10^{3}\ \text{kPa cm}^3$ ✓ (accept 2.3–2.5)
- it is the constant $p(V + V_0)$, i.e. $nRT$ for the trapped air ✓

**(d)**
- $nRT = 2.4\times10^{3}\ \text{kPa cm}^3 = 2.4\times10^{3}\times10^{3}\times10^{-6} = 2.4\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $n = \dfrac{2.4}{8.31 \times 293} = 9.9\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$ ✓

ECF from (c)(ii). Award [1 max] for a power-of-ten error in the unit conversion.

**(e)**
- compressing a gas does work on it; doing it slowly allows energy to be transferred to the surroundings so the temperature stays constant ✓

text:
A fixed mass of air is held at a constant volume of $250\ \text{cm}^3$. Its pressure $p$ is measured at different Celsius temperatures $\theta$.

| $\theta$ / °C | 10 | 30 | 50 | 70 | 90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p$ / kPa | 103.7 | 110.9 | 118.4 | 125.6 | 133.0 |

(a) The relationship between $p$ and $\theta$ is linear. Use the data to estimate the value of absolute zero in °C. [3]

(b) Determine the amount, in mol, of air in the container. [2]

(c) Calculate the mean kinetic energy of the air molecules at 90 °C. [2]

(d) Explain, using the kinetic model, why the pressure of the air increases when it is heated at constant volume. [3]
ms:
**(a)**
- gradient $= \dfrac{133.0 - 103.7}{90 - 10} = 0.366\ \text{kPa K}^{-1}$ ✓
- pressure at 0 °C $= 103.7 - 10 \times 0.366 = 100.0\ \text{kPa}$ ✓
- $p = 0$ when $\theta = -\dfrac{100.0}{0.366} = -273\ \text{°C}$ ✓

Accept −270 °C to −276 °C. Accept an equivalent method, e.g. a best-fit line.

**(b)**
- $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = \dfrac{103.7\times10^{3} \times 250\times10^{-6}}{8.31 \times 283}$ ✓
- $0.011\ \text{mol}$ ✓

Any data pair may be used. Award [1 max] if the Celsius temperature is used.

**(c)**
