What is the new force between the charges?

A. $\dfrac{F}{4}$
B. $\dfrac{F}{2}$
C. $F$
D. $2F$
ms: $F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}$: the product of charges increases by 4 and $r^2$ increases by 4, so $F$ is unchanged. A ignores the change in charges; B and D come from treating the dependence on $r$ or $q$ as linear.

text:
The diagram shows the electric field lines around two point charges X and Y.

![Electric field lines around two point charges X and Y, with arrows](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.2_2.svg)

Which statement about X and Y is correct?

A. X is positive, Y is negative and the magnitudes of the charges are equal.
B. X is positive, Y is negative and X has the larger magnitude.
C. X is negative, Y is positive and X has the larger magnitude.
D. X is negative, Y is positive and the magnitudes of the charges are equal.
ms: Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, so X is positive and Y negative. More lines leave X than end on Y (some lines from X go off to infinity), so $|q_X| > |q_Y|$. A would require every line from X to end on Y.

text:
Two long, straight, parallel wires are a distance $d$ apart in a vacuum. They carry equal currents $I$ in opposite directions. The magnetic field strength at a perpendicular distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

What is the magnitude of the magnetic field strength at the point midway between the wires?

A. zero
B. $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$
C. $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi d}$
D. $\dfrac{2\mu_0 I}{\pi d}$
ms: Each wire gives $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(d/2)} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi d}$; for opposite currents the fields at the midpoint are in the same direction, so they add to $\dfrac{2\mu_0 I}{\pi d}$. A is correct only for currents in the same direction; C is the field of one wire; B is the field of one wire calculated with distance $d$ instead of $d/2$.

text:
A negatively charged rod is held close to, but not touching, an uncharged metal sphere on an insulating stand. With the rod still in place, the sphere is connected to earth for a moment. The earth connection is then removed, and finally the rod is taken away.

What is the final charge on the sphere and why?

A. positive, because electrons flowed from the sphere to earth
B. negative, because electrons flowed from earth to the sphere
C. positive, because positive charge flowed from earth to the sphere
D. zero, because the rod never touched the sphere
ms: The negative rod repels free electrons in the sphere; when earthed, some electrons flow to earth. With the earth removed first, the sphere is left with a deficit of electrons, i.e. a net positive charge (charge is conserved overall). C is wrong because only electrons move in metals; D ignores charging by induction.

text:
Which statements about electric equipotential surfaces are correct?

I. Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
II. No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
III. The electric field strength is greatest where the equipotential surfaces are furthest apart.

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: $E = -\dfrac{\Delta V_\text{e}}{\Delta r}$: field lines cross equipotentials at right angles and $W = q\Delta V_\text{e} = 0$ along one. Where equipotentials (at equal intervals of $V$) are closer, the potential gradient and so the field strength are greater, so III is false.

text:
A point charge $+Q$ is fixed at X and a point charge $-2Q$ is fixed at Y. The distance XY is $d$.

At which point on the straight line between X and Y is the electric potential zero?

A. a distance $\dfrac{d}{3}$ from X
B. a distance $\dfrac{2d}{3}$ from X
C. a distance $(\sqrt{2}-1)d$ from X
D. There is no such point between X and Y.
ms: $\dfrac{kQ}{x} - \dfrac{2kQ}{d-x} = 0$ gives $d - x = 2x$, so $x = \dfrac{d}{3}$ (closer to the smaller charge). C comes from equating field strengths (inverse-square), which actually gives no zero-field point between opposite charges; D confuses potential with field strength. B places it nearer the larger charge.

text:
A student investigates the magnetic field near a long straight wire carrying a constant current of 5.0 A. A calibrated magnetic field probe measures the field strength $B$ at different perpendicular distances $r$ from the wire. The uncertainty in each value of $B$ is $\pm2\ \mu\text{T}$.

| $r$ / cm | 1.00 | 1.50 | 2.00 | 3.00 | 4.00 | 5.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $B$ / $\mu$T | 104 | 71 | 54 | 37 | 29 | 24 |

The student plots a graph of $B$ against $\dfrac{1}{r}$. The field of a long straight wire is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

![Graph of B in microtesla against 1/r with a straight best-fit line that does not pass through the origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.2_7.svg)

(a) Explain why the student plots $B$ against $\dfrac{1}{r}$ rather than $B$ against $r$. [1]

(b) Use the graph to determine a value for the magnetic permeability of free space $\mu_0$. [3]

(c) The best-fit line does not pass through the origin.

(i) Suggest one reason for this. [1]

(ii) State and explain the effect, if any, of this on the value of $\mu_0$ obtained in (b). [1]

(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $B$ at $r = 5.00$ cm. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ so $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$ and this graph should be a straight line (whose gradient gives $\mu_0$) ✓

(b)
- gradient from a large triangle, e.g. $\dfrac{(104-24)\times10^{-6}}{100-20} = 1.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{T m}$ ✓
- gradient $= \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}$ so $\mu_0 = \dfrac{2\pi\times\text{gradient}}{I}$ ✓
- $\mu_0 = 1.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{T m A}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept $1.2\times10^{-6}$ to $1.3\times10^{-6}$; accept units H m$^{-1}$ or N A$^{-2}$)
- Award [2 max] if $\mu$T is not converted to T.

(c)(i)
- a constant background field (e.g. the Earth's magnetic field) is added to every reading / probe not zeroed: a systematic error ✓

(c)(ii)
- no effect, because a systematic offset shifts the line without changing its gradient ✓

(d)
- $\dfrac{2}{24}\times100 = 8\%$ ✓ (accept 8.3%)

text:
Two small charged spheres A and B are fixed 0.30 m apart in a vacuum. A has charge $+4.0\ \mu\text{C}$ and B has charge $-6.0\ \mu\text{C}$. Point P lies on the line AB, 0.10 m from A.

![Charges +4.0 microcoulomb at A and -6.0 microcoulomb at B, 0.30 m apart, with point P 0.10 m from A](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.2_8.svg)

(a) Calculate the magnitude of the electric force between A and B. [2]

(b) Determine the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field strength at P. [3]

(c) An electron is placed at P. Calculate the magnitude of the force on the electron and state its direction. [2]

(d) The spheres are identical. They are made to touch briefly and are then returned to their original positions. State the charge now on each sphere, and outline the principle you used. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times4.0\times10^{-6}\times6.0\times10^{-6}}{0.30^2}$ ✓
- $F = 2.4\ \text{N}$ ✓

(b)
- field due to A at P $= \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times4.0\times10^{-6}}{0.10^2} = 3.6\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ (towards B) ✓
- field due to B at P $= \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times6.0\times10^{-6}}{0.20^2} = 1.35\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ (towards B) ✓
- both point towards B so they add: $E = 4.9\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$ towards B ✓
- Award [2 max] for subtracting the fields ($2.2\times10^{6}$ N C$^{-1}$).

(c)
- $F = eE = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times4.9\times10^{6} = 7.9\times10^{-13}\ \text{N}$ ✓
- towards A (opposite to the field) ✓
- Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- each sphere has charge $-1.0\ \mu\text{C}$ ✓
- conservation of charge: total charge $-2.0\ \mu$C is shared equally between identical spheres ✓

text:
A solenoid of length 0.25 m has 500 turns and carries a current of 2.0 A. It is in air.

The magnetic field strength inside a long solenoid of length $L$ with $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{L}$. The magnetic field strength at a perpendicular distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

(a) Sketch the magnetic field pattern inside and around the solenoid. [2]

(b) Calculate the magnetic field strength near the centre of the solenoid. [2]

(c) The solenoid is replaced by one with the same number of turns and the same current but twice the length. State the new magnetic field strength near the centre. [1]

(d) A long straight wire carries a current of 12 A. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field at the location is $5.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$. Calculate the distance from the wire at which the magnetic field due to the wire has the same magnitude as this component. [2]
ms:
(a)
- parallel, equally spaced lines inside the solenoid along its axis ✓
- lines emerge from one end and loop round outside to the other end, like a bar magnet's field, forming closed loops; directions consistent (inside: from S end to N end) ✓

(b)
- $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{L} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times500\times2.0}{0.25}$ ✓
- $B = 5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}$ ✓

(c)
- $2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}$ (half of the value in (b)) ✓ Allow ECF.

(d)
- $r = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi B} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times12}{2\pi\times5.0\times10^{-5}}$ ✓
- $r = 0.048\ \text{m}$ ✓

text:
In a scattering experiment an alpha particle (charge $+2e$) with initial kinetic energy 5.0 MeV is fired directly towards a stationary gold nucleus (charge $+79e$). The gold nucleus may be assumed to remain at rest and both particles may be treated as point charges.

(a) Define electric potential at a point. [2]

(b) Show that the distance of closest approach of the alpha particle to the centre of the gold nucleus is about $5\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}$. [3]

(c) Calculate the electric potential due to the gold nucleus at the point of closest approach. [2]

(d) A second alpha particle with the same initial kinetic energy is not aimed directly at the nucleus. Explain why its minimum distance from the nucleus is greater than the value in (b). [2]
ms:
(a)
- the work done per unit (positive) charge ✓
- in bringing a small positive test charge from infinity to that point ✓

(b)
- initial kinetic energy $= 5.0\times10^{6}\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 8.0\times10^{-13}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- at closest approach all kinetic energy is converted to electric potential energy: $\dfrac{k(2e)(79e)}{r} = 8.0\times10^{-13}$ ✓
- $r = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times2\times79\times(1.60\times10^{-19})^2}{8.0\times10^{-13}} = 4.5\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- $V_\text{e} = \dfrac{kQ}{r} = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times79\times1.60\times10^{-19}}{4.5\times10^{-14}}$ ✓
- $V_\text{e} = 2.5\times10^{6}\ \text{V}$ ✓
- Alternative: $V_\text{e} = \dfrac{E_\text{p}}{q} = \dfrac{8.0\times10^{-13}}{2\times1.60\times10^{-19}}$. Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- the particle still has a velocity component perpendicular to the line to the nucleus at closest approach, so it still has kinetic energy there ✓
- so less kinetic energy is converted to electric potential energy, so $E_\text{p}$ is smaller and $r$ is larger ✓

text:
The diagram shows four equipotential lines around an isolated positive point charge Q in a vacuum. The values of the electric potential are shown. Points A and B lie on equipotentials.

![Circular equipotentials of 900 V, 600 V, 450 V and 300 V around a point charge Q at the origin, with A at 10 cm and B at 30 cm](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.2_11.svg)

(a) Use the diagram to determine the charge Q. [2]

(b) Calculate the work done by an external force in moving a charge of $+2.0\ \text{nC}$ slowly from B to A. [2]

(c) Estimate, using the diagram, the electric field strength at a distance of 17.5 cm from Q. [2]

(d) Explain why the spacing between these equipotential lines increases with distance from Q. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $V_\text{e} = \dfrac{kQ}{r}$, e.g. $900 = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\,Q}{0.10}$ ✓
- $Q = 1.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{C}$ ✓

(b)
- $W = q\Delta V_\text{e} = 2.0\times10^{-9}\times(900 - 300)$ ✓
- $W = 1.2\times10^{-6}\ \text{J}$ ✓

(c)
- $E \approx \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta r} = \dfrac{600 - 450}{0.20 - 0.15}$ ✓
- $E \approx 3.0\times10^{3}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept 2.9 to 3.0 kV m$^{-1}$, e.g. from $\dfrac{kQ}{r^2}$)

(d)
- the field strength decreases with distance (inverse-square law) ✓
- since $E = -\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}$, a larger distance $\Delta r$ is needed for the same change in potential / the potential decreases as $\dfrac{1}{r}$ so equal steps of $V$ need increasing steps of $r$ ✓

text:
An electron moves with speed $3.0\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.20 T.

What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the electron?

A. zero
B. $4.8\times10^{-14}\ \text{N}$
C. $9.6\times10^{-14}\ \text{N}$
D. $9.6\times10^{-20}\ \text{N}$
ms: $F = qvB\sin\theta = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times3.0\times10^{6}\times0.20\times\sin90^\circ = 9.6\times10^{-14}\ \text{N}$. A is for motion parallel to the field; B uses $\sin30^\circ$; D omits the speed's power of ten.

text:
A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same speed, moving at right angles to the field.

What is $\dfrac{\text{radius of path of alpha particle}}{\text{radius of path of proton}}$?

A. $\dfrac{1}{2}$
B. 1
C. 2
D. 4
ms: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$; the alpha particle has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge, so its radius is $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2$ times larger. D ignores the charge; A inverts the ratio.

text:
A straight wire carrying a current into the page is placed between the poles of a magnet, as shown.

![Wire carrying current into the page between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.3_3.svg)

What is the direction of the magnetic force on the wire?

A. towards the top of the page
B. towards the bottom of the page
C. towards the N pole
D. towards the S pole
ms: The field is from N to S (left to right). With current into the page, the left-hand rule (or $\vec F = I\vec L \times \vec B$) gives a force towards the bottom of the page. C and D wrongly put the force along the field; A results from reversing the current or field.

text:
A beam of positive ions passes undeflected through a region where a uniform electric field of strength $2.0\times10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.050 T. The ions move perpendicular to both fields.

What is the speed of the ions?

A. $1.0\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
B. $2.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
C. $4.0\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$
D. It depends on the charge of the ions.
ms: Undeflected means $qE = qvB$, so $v = \dfrac{E}{B} = \dfrac{2.0\times10^{4}}{0.050} = 4.0\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, independent of $q$ and $m$. A multiplies $E$ and $B$; B inverts the ratio; D misses that $q$ cancels.

text:
A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. Its speed is doubled without changing the field.

Which statements are correct?

I. The radius of the circle doubles.
II. The time for one revolution is unchanged.
III. The kinetic energy of the particle doubles.

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} \propto v$, so I is true. $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ is independent of speed, so II is true. Kinetic energy $\propto v^2$ quadruples, so III is false.

text:
Two long, parallel wires P and Q carry currents in the same direction. The current in P is $3I$ and the current in Q is $I$. The magnetic force on a 1.0 m length of Q is $F$.

What is the magnetic force on a 1.0 m length of P?

A. $F$, attractive
B. $3F$, attractive
C. $F$, repulsive
D. $\dfrac{F}{3}$, repulsive
ms: $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$ is the same for both wires (Newton's third law), and currents in the same direction attract. B assumes the force depends only on the wire's own current; C and D get the direction wrong.

text:
In an experiment to measure the specific charge $\dfrac{e}{m_\text{e}}$ of the electron, electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$. They then enter a uniform magnetic field of strength $1.00\ \text{mT}$ at right angles to their velocity and move in a circle of radius $r$. The table gives the results; the uncertainty in each value of $r$ is $\pm0.05$ cm.

| $V$ / V | 150 | 200 | 250 | 300 | 350 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $r$ / cm | 4.13 | 4.77 | 5.33 | 5.84 | 6.31 |

The graph shows $r^2$ plotted against $V$.

![Graph of r squared against accelerating potential difference V, a straight line through the origin](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.3_7.svg)

(a) Show that $r^2 = \dfrac{2m_\text{e}}{eB^2}V$. [2]

(b) Use the graph to determine $\dfrac{e}{m_\text{e}}$. [3]

(c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $r^2$ for $V = 150$ V. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $eV = \tfrac{1}{2}m_\text{e}v^2$ and $evB = \dfrac{m_\text{e}v^2}{r}$ (so $r = \dfrac{m_\text{e}v}{eB}$) ✓
- eliminating $v$: $r^2 = \dfrac{m_\text{e}^2}{e^2B^2}\times\dfrac{2eV}{m_\text{e}} = \dfrac{2m_\text{e}}{eB^2}V$ ✓

(b)
- gradient, e.g. $\dfrac{4.0\times10^{-3}}{350} = 1.14\times10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2\ \text{V}^{-1}$ ✓
- $\dfrac{e}{m_\text{e}} = \dfrac{2}{B^2\times\text{gradient}} = \dfrac{2}{(1.00\times10^{-3})^2\times1.14\times10^{-5}}$ ✓
- $\dfrac{e}{m_\text{e}} = 1.8\times10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept 1.7 to $1.8\times10^{11}$)

(c)
- $2\times\dfrac{0.05}{4.13}\times100 = 2.4\%$ ✓ (accept 2%)

text:
An electron enters the region between two parallel metal plates in a vacuum, midway between them and moving parallel to them with speed $2.5\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The plates are 6.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart, with a potential difference of 150 V between them. Assume the field is uniform between the plates and zero outside, and ignore gravity.

![Electron entering midway between parallel plates 6.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart, top plate +150 V, bottom plate 0 V](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.3_8.svg)

(a) Calculate the magnitude of the electric force on the electron between the plates. [2]

(b) Calculate the time the electron spends between the plates. [1]

(c) Show that the electron leaves the plates without hitting the upper plate, and state the vertical displacement as it leaves. [3]

(d) Describe the path of the electron after it leaves the region between the plates. [1]

(e) An electron with half the initial speed enters at the same point. Determine whether it strikes a plate. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $E = \dfrac{V}{d} = \dfrac{150}{0.020} = 7.5\times10^{3}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$ ✓
- $F = eE = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times7.5\times10^{3} = 1.2\times10^{-15}\ \text{N}$ ✓

(b)
- $t = \dfrac{0.060}{2.5\times10^{7}} = 2.4\times10^{-9}\ \text{s}$ ✓

(c)
- $a = \dfrac{F}{m_\text{e}} = \dfrac{1.2\times10^{-15}}{9.11\times10^{-31}} = 1.3\times10^{15}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (towards the positive plate) ✓
- $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times1.32\times10^{15}\times(2.4\times10^{-9})^2 = 3.8\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}$ ✓
- 3.8 mm is less than the 10 mm gap between the electron's initial line and the upper plate, so it emerges ✓
- Allow ECF from (a) and (b).

(d)
- a straight line (at constant velocity), at an angle to its original direction (deflected towards the upper side) ✓

(e)
- time between the plates doubles, so the deflection would be $4\times3.8 = 15\ \text{mm}$ (or calculated) ✓
- 15 mm > 10 mm, so it strikes the upper (positive) plate ✓

text:
A proton travelling at $4.0\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ enters a region of uniform magnetic field at point E. The field has strength 0.35 T and is directed into the page. The proton's velocity at E is perpendicular to the boundary of the field.

![Proton moving to the right entering a uniform magnetic field into the page at point E on a vertical boundary](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.3_9.svg)

(a) State the direction of the magnetic force on the proton at E, and explain why the proton moves in a circular arc. [3]

(b) Calculate the radius of the path of the proton. [2]

(c) Calculate the time the proton spends in the magnetic field. [2]

(d) An electron enters the field at E with the same velocity. State two ways in which its path differs from that of the proton. [2]
ms:
(a)
- towards the top of the page (perpendicular to the velocity) ✓
- the force is always perpendicular to the velocity so it changes direction but not speed/does no work ✓
- the force has constant magnitude ($qvB$, speed constant) so it provides a centripetal force ✓

(b)
- $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{1.67\times10^{-27}\times4.0\times10^{6}}{1.60\times10^{-19}\times0.35}$ ✓
- $r = 0.12\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- the proton completes a semicircle and leaves the field through the boundary ✓
- $t = \dfrac{\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{\pi m}{qB} = 9.4\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (b). Award [1 max] for a full period ($1.9\times10^{-7}$ s).

(d)
- curves in the opposite direction (downwards) ✓
- much smaller radius ($6.5\times10^{-5}$ m / about 1800 times smaller) ✓

text:
Two long, straight, parallel wires X and Y are 4.0 cm apart in air. X carries a current of 8.0 A and Y carries a current of 5.0 A in the opposite direction.

The magnetic field strength at a perpendicular distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$.

(a) Calculate the magnetic field strength due to X at the position of Y. [2]

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on a 1.5 m length of Y. [2]

(c) State whether the force between the wires is attractive or repulsive, and explain why the force on 1.5 m of X has the same magnitude as the force in (b). [2]

(d) Determine the position, in the plane of the wires, at which the resultant magnetic field due to the two wires is zero. [3]
ms:
(a)
- $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times8.0}{2\pi\times0.040}$ ✓
- $B = 4.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{T}$ ✓

(b)
- $F = BIL = 4.0\times10^{-5}\times5.0\times1.5$ (or $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1I_2L}{2\pi r}$) ✓
- $F = 3.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{N}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- repulsive (currents in opposite directions) ✓
- Newton's third law: the forces are an interaction pair / $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$ is symmetric in the two currents ✓

(d)
- between the wires the fields are in the same direction so the zero point must be outside, on the side of the smaller current (beyond Y) ✓
- $\dfrac{8.0}{x + 0.040} = \dfrac{5.0}{x}$ where $x$ is the distance from Y ✓
- $x = 0.067\ \text{m}$, i.e. 6.7 cm from Y (10.7 cm from X), on the side away from X ✓

text:
A flat coil of 200 turns and area $0.050\ \text{m}^2$ is in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.40 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the direction of the field.

What is the magnetic flux linkage through the coil?

A. $0.010\ \text{Wb}$
B. $1.7\ \text{Wb}$
C. $2.0\ \text{Wb}$
D. $3.5\ \text{Wb}$
ms: The angle between the field and the normal to the coil is $60^\circ$, so $N\Phi = NBA\cos60^\circ = 200\times0.40\times0.050\times0.5 = 2.0\ \text{Wb}$. D uses $\cos30^\circ$ (the angle to the plane); A is the flux through one turn; B halves the wrong value.

text:
The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards end X of a coil that is connected to a resistor.

Which describes the magnetic polarity induced at end X and the force on the magnet?

A. north pole; the magnet is repelled
B. south pole; the magnet is attracted
C. north pole; the magnet is attracted
D. south pole; the magnet is repelled
ms: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change causing it, so X becomes a north pole and repels the approaching north pole. B would make the magnet speed up and create energy from nothing; C and D are inconsistent combinations.

text:
The graph shows how the magnetic flux through each turn of a 50-turn coil varies with time.

![Graph of flux in milliweber against time: rises from 0 to 60 mWb between 0 and 2 s, constant until 4 s, falls to 0 at 5 s](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.4_3.svg)

What is the greatest magnitude of the induced emf, and when does it occur?

A. 1.5 V, between 0 and 2 s
B. 3.0 V, between 4 s and 5 s
C. 0.060 V, between 4 s and 5 s
D. 3.0 V, between 2 s and 4 s
ms: $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$: the steepest gradient is from 4 s to 5 s, $\dfrac{0.060}{1.0} = 0.060\ \text{Wb s}^{-1}$, so $\varepsilon = 50\times0.060 = 3.0\ \text{V}$. A is the emf during 0 to 2 s (smaller gradient); C forgets the 50 turns; D confuses maximum flux with maximum rate of change of flux (the emf is zero from 2 s to 4 s).

text:
A simple AC generator consists of a coil rotating at a constant rate in a uniform magnetic field. The rate of rotation is doubled.

What happens to the peak emf and to the frequency of the output?

A. peak emf unchanged; frequency doubled
B. peak emf doubled; frequency doubled
C. peak emf doubled; frequency unchanged
D. peak emf quadrupled; frequency doubled
ms: Doubling the rotation rate halves the time for each change of flux linkage, so the rate of change of flux (peak emf) doubles, and there are twice as many cycles per second. A ignores Faraday's law; D squares the factor.

text:
A metal rod of length 0.25 m slides at a constant speed of $4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ along two parallel horizontal rails that are connected by a resistor. The total resistance of the circuit is $2.0\ \Omega$. A uniform vertical magnetic field of strength 0.50 T acts on the rod. Friction is negligible.

What is the horizontal force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed?

A. $0.031\ \text{N}$
B. $0.063\ \text{N}$
C. $0.13\ \text{N}$
D. $0.50\ \text{N}$
ms: $\varepsilon = BvL = 0.50\times4.0\times0.25 = 0.50\ \text{V}$, $I = \dfrac{0.50}{2.0} = 0.25\ \text{A}$, and the applied force balances $BIL = 0.50\times0.25\times0.25 = 0.031\ \text{N}$ (check: $Fv = 0.125\ \text{W} = \dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{R}$). B uses the emf as if it were the current ($I = 0.50$ A); C is the power in watts; D is the emf in volts.

text:
A small bar magnet is released from rest above a horizontal coil of 400 turns and falls vertically through it. The coil is connected to a data logger, which records the induced emf. Air resistance is negligible.

![Graph of induced emf against time: a positive peak of 0.30 V at about 144 ms, zero at about 156 ms, then a negative peak of about -0.35 V at about 170 ms](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.4_6.svg)

(a) Explain why the emf is zero at about $t = 156$ ms. [2]

(b) Explain why the negative peak is larger in magnitude and narrower than the positive peak. [2]

(c) Explain why the emf changes sign. [1]

(d) The area between the curve and the time axis is approximately the same for the positive and the negative parts of the graph. By estimating one of these areas, determine the maximum magnetic flux through one turn of the coil. [2]
ms:
(a)
- the magnet is at the centre of the coil where the flux linkage is a maximum ✓
- the rate of change of flux linkage is momentarily zero, so by Faraday's law $\varepsilon = 0$ ✓

(b)
- the magnet is accelerating so it moves faster as it leaves the coil ✓
- the flux changes at a greater rate, giving a larger emf over a shorter time ✓

(c)
- the flux through the coil increases as the magnet enters but decreases as it leaves, so the rate of change of flux (and the induced current, by Lenz's law) reverses ✓

(d)
- area estimated, e.g. by counting squares or a triangle: approximately $0.5\times0.30\times0.065 \approx 1\times10^{-2}\ \text{V s}$ (accept $0.8\times10^{-2}$ to $1.2\times10^{-2}$ V s); this equals the maximum flux linkage $N\Phi$ ✓
- $\Phi = \dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{400} = 2.5\times10^{-5}\ \text{Wb}$ ✓ (accept $2\times10^{-5}$ to $3\times10^{-5}$ Wb)

text:
A square coil PQRS of 20 turns and side 5.0 cm is pulled at a constant speed of $0.20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ out of a region of uniform magnetic field of strength 0.60 T. The field is directed into the page. The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, and side QR has already left the field, as shown. The total resistance of the coil is $0.80\ \Omega$.

![Square coil PQRS moving right at 0.20 m/s, partly out of a magnetic field into the page of 0.60 T](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.4_7.svg)

(a) Calculate the emf induced in the coil while it is leaving the field. [2]

(b) Determine the direction of the induced current in side PS, and explain your answer. [3]

(c) Calculate the force needed to pull the coil at constant speed. [2]

(d) Show that the work done by this force while the coil leaves the field equals the electrical energy dissipated in the coil. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\varepsilon = NBvL = 20\times0.60\times0.20\times0.050$ ✓
- $\varepsilon = 0.12\ \text{V}$ ✓

(b)
- the flux (into the page) through the coil is decreasing ✓
- by Lenz's law the induced current produces a field into the page inside the coil, so it flows clockwise (as viewed) ✓
- so in PS the current flows from S to P (up the page) ✓
- Alternative using the force on PS: current in PS must make the force on PS oppose the motion (to the left), giving S to P.

(c)
- $I = \dfrac{0.12}{0.80} = 0.15\ \text{A}$ ✓
- $F = NBIL = 20\times0.60\times0.15\times0.050 = 0.090\ \text{N}$ ✓
- Allow ECF from (a).

(d)
- work done $= Fd = 0.090\times0.050 = 4.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- time $= \dfrac{0.050}{0.20} = 0.25$ s; energy dissipated $= \varepsilon It = 0.12\times0.15\times0.25 = 4.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}$ ✓

text:
A coil of 150 turns, each of area $4.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$, rotates at a constant rate in a uniform magnetic field. The graph shows how the emf $\varepsilon$ induced in the coil varies with time $t$.

![Sinusoidal emf against time with peak 12 V and period 20 ms, from 0 to 40 ms](qbank/img/gen_phys_D.4_8.svg)

(a) Determine the frequency of rotation of the coil. [1]

(b) State the orientation of the plane of the coil relative to the magnetic field when the emf is at its maximum, and explain your answer. [2]

(c) The peak emf of a coil rotating with angular frequency $\omega$ is given by $\varepsilon_0 = \omega NBA$. Determine the magnetic field strength. [2]

(d) The frequency of rotation is halved. Sketch, on the same axes, the variation of the new emf with time from $t = 0$ to $t = 40$ ms. [2]

(e) State the value of the magnetic flux linkage through the coil when the emf is at its maximum. [1]
ms:
(a)
- period $= 20$ ms so $f = 50\ \text{Hz}$ ✓

(b)
- the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field ✓
- the flux linkage is zero at this moment but is changing at its greatest rate (the sides of the coil cut the field lines at the greatest rate) ✓

(c)
- $\omega = 2\pi\times50 = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ and $B = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0}{\omega NA} = \dfrac{12}{314\times150\times4.0\times10^{-3}}$ ✓
- $B = 0.064\ \text{T}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a).

(d)
- sinusoidal curve with peak 6 V ✓
- period 40 ms (one complete cycle between 0 and 40 ms, starting at zero) ✓

(e)
- zero ✓

text:
A long solenoid of length 0.40 m has 800 turns and is in air. A small flat coil of 120 turns, each of area $4.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$, is placed at the centre of the solenoid with its plane perpendicular to the axis of the solenoid. The current in the solenoid increases uniformly from zero to 3.0 A in 0.15 s and then remains constant.

The magnetic field strength inside a long solenoid of length $L$ with $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{L}$.

(a) Calculate the magnetic field strength at the centre of the solenoid when the current is 3.0 A. [2]

(b) Determine the emf induced in the small coil while the current is increasing. [3]

(c) Explain, with reference to Lenz's law, the direction of the induced current in the small coil compared with the current in the solenoid. [2]

(d) Sketch a graph showing how the emf induced in the small coil varies with time from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.30$ s. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{L} = \dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times800\times3.0}{0.40}$ ✓
- $B = 7.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{T}$ ✓

(b)
- rate of change of field $= \dfrac{7.5\times10^{-3}}{0.15} = 5.0\times10^{-2}\ \text{T s}^{-1}$ ✓
- $\varepsilon = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = NA\dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} = 120\times4.0\times10^{-4}\times5.0\times10^{-2}$ ✓
- $\varepsilon = 2.4\times10^{-3}\ \text{V}$ ✓ Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- the induced current opposes the increase in flux through the small coil ✓
- so it produces a field opposite to the solenoid's field, i.e. it circulates in the opposite sense to the solenoid current ✓

(d)
- constant (non-zero) emf of 2.4 mV from 0 to 0.15 s ✓
- emf falls to zero at 0.15 s and stays at zero to 0.30 s ✓

text:
In the Geiger–Marsden experiment, alpha particles were directed at a thin gold foil. Most of the alpha particles passed through the foil with little or no deviation.

What does this observation suggest?

A. Most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
B. Most of the volume of the atom is empty space.
C. The nucleus is positively charged.
D. Electrons orbit the nucleus in discrete energy levels.
ms: **B.** Undeflected passage of most alpha particles means they met nothing that could exert a large force on them: the atom is mostly empty space. A and C are conclusions drawn from the *small number of large-angle* deflections, not from the undeflected majority. D is not tested by this experiment at all.

text:
The diagram shows some of the energy levels of the hydrogen atom.

![energy levels n = 1 to 4 and n = infinity of hydrogen](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.1_2.svg)

A large number of hydrogen atoms are excited to the $n = 4$ level. How many different wavelengths of photon can be emitted as the atoms return to the ground state?

A. 3
B. 4
C. 6
D. 10
ms: **C.** Possible transitions: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1, 2→1 = 6, each with a different energy difference and therefore a different wavelength. A counts only single-step cascades from $n=4$ down; B counts the levels; D wrongly adds 4 + 3 + 2 + 1.

text:
The radius of a nucleus is given by $R = R_0A^{\frac{1}{3}}$. Nucleus X has nucleon number 27 and nucleus Y has nucleon number 216.

What are $\dfrac{\text{radius of Y}}{\text{radius of X}}$ and $\dfrac{\text{density of Y}}{\text{density of X}}$?

A. radius ratio 2, density ratio 1
B. radius ratio 2, density ratio $\frac{1}{8}$
C. radius ratio 8, density ratio 1
D. radius ratio 8, density ratio $\frac{1}{8}$
ms: **A.** $R_Y/R_X = (216/27)^{1/3} = 8^{1/3} = 2$. Mass $\propto A$ and volume $\propto R^3 \propto A$, so nuclear density is independent of $A$: ratio 1. C forgets the cube root; B and D wrongly assume density changes (mass ratio 8 divided by volume ratio 8 gives 1, not 1/8).

text:
White light from a hot source passes through a cool gas of hydrogen and is then analysed with a spectrometer. Dark lines appear in the spectrum.

Which statement best explains the dark lines?

A. The cool gas emits photons only at the wavelengths of the dark lines.
B. Photons at those wavelengths are diffracted by the atoms in the gas.
C. Atoms in the gas absorb all photons with energies greater than the ionisation energy.
D. Atoms in the gas absorb photons whose energies equal differences between their energy levels, and re-emit them in all directions.
ms: **D.** Only photons with energy exactly equal to an energy-level difference are absorbed; the re-emission is in random directions, so the intensity in the original direction is reduced at those wavelengths. A describes an emission spectrum (bright lines). C would give a continuous absorption region, not lines. B is irrelevant: atoms do not diffract light selectively at these wavelengths.

text:
In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the electron moves from the orbit with $n = 1$ to the orbit with $n = 2$.

By what factors do the radius of the orbit and the speed of the electron change?

A. radius × 2, speed × $\frac{1}{2}$
B. radius × 4, speed × $\frac{1}{4}$
C. radius × 2, speed × 2
D. radius × 4, speed × $\frac{1}{2}$
ms: **D.** From $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$ and $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{ke^2}{r^2}$: $r \propto n^2$ and $v = \dfrac{2\pi ke^2}{nh} \propto \dfrac{1}{n}$. So the radius increases by 4 and the speed halves. B confuses speed with kinetic or total energy (which $\propto 1/n^2$); A assumes $r \propto n$.

text:
The visible part of the emission spectrum of atomic hydrogen contains four lines, shown below.

![hydrogen emission lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.1_6.svg)

The table gives some energy levels of hydrogen.

| level | energy / eV |
|---|---|
| ground state | −13.6 |
| first excited state | −3.40 |
| second excited state | −1.51 |
| third excited state | −0.85 |

(a) Calculate, in eV, the energy of a photon of the 486 nm line. [2]

(b) All four visible lines are produced by transitions that end on the first excited state. Using your answer to (a), identify the level in which the transition producing the 486 nm line starts. [2]

(c) Explain why the emission spectrum of hydrogen consists of discrete lines rather than a continuous band. [2]

(d) State one feature of the spectrum that would be observed if white light were passed through cool hydrogen gas instead. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{486\times10^{-9}} = 4.09\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $= \dfrac{4.09\times10^{-19}}{1.60\times10^{-19}} = 2.56\ \text{eV}$ ✓

Award [2] for a correct final answer. Award [1] max for an answer left in J.

(b)
- energy of upper level $= -3.40 + 2.56 = -0.84\ \text{eV}$ ✓
- this matches the third excited state (−0.85 eV) / $n = 4$ ✓

Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- electrons in atoms can only occupy discrete energy levels / atomic energy is quantized ✓
- a photon is emitted with energy equal to the difference between two levels, so only specific photon energies/wavelengths (via $E = hf$) occur ✓

(d)
- dark (absorption) lines on a continuous spectrum at the same wavelengths (410, 434, 486, 656 nm) as the emission lines ✓

text:
The diagram shows the paths of three alpha particles, labelled 1, 2 and 3, approaching a gold nucleus in a Geiger–Marsden type experiment. Particle 3 is moving directly towards the nucleus.

![paths of three alpha particles near a nucleus with different deflections](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.1_7.svg)

(a) Outline **two** observations made in the Geiger–Marsden experiment and, for each, the conclusion drawn about the structure of the atom. [4]

(b) With reference to the diagram, explain why particle 2 is deflected through a larger angle than particle 1. [2]

(c) State why the gold foil used in the experiment had to be very thin. [1]
ms:
(a) Any two observation–conclusion pairs, [1] for each observation and [1] for the matching conclusion:
- most alpha particles passed straight through/undeflected ✓ → most of the atom is empty space ✓
- a small number were deflected through large angles/some bounced back (more than 90°) ✓ → the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus ✓
- the number deflected decreased rapidly as the angle increased ✓ → the nucleus is very small compared with the atom ✓

(b)
- particle 2 passes closer to the nucleus ✓
- so the (Coulomb) repulsive force on it is larger (force $\propto 1/r^2$) and acts in a more sideways direction, giving a greater change of momentum ✓

(c)
- so that each alpha particle is scattered by only one nucleus / to avoid multiple scattering / so alpha particles are not absorbed in the foil ✓

text:
Alpha particles of kinetic energy 7.7 MeV are fired head-on at gold-197 nuclei ($^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$). Assume the gold nucleus does not recoil.

(a) Show that the distance of closest approach of the alpha particles to the centre of a gold nucleus is about $3\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}$. [2]

(b) Calculate the radius of a gold-197 nucleus, using $R_0 = 1.20\times10^{-15}\ \text{m}$. [1]

(c) Determine the minimum kinetic energy, in MeV, an alpha particle would need to reach the surface of the gold nucleus. Treat the alpha particle as a point charge. [2]

(d) Experiments with alpha particles of energy much greater than your answer to (c) show scattering that deviates from the predictions of Rutherford's model. Explain this observation. [2]

(e) Show that the density of a nucleus does not depend on its nucleon number $A$, and estimate the nuclear density. [3]
ms:
(a)
- $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{kQq}{d}$ with $Q = 79e$, $q = 2e$, $E_\text{k} = 7.7\times10^{6}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $d = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times79\times2\times(1.60\times10^{-19})^2}{7.7\times10^{6}\times1.60\times10^{-19}} = 2.95\times10^{-14}\ \text{m}$ ✓

At least 2 s.f. must be shown for the "show that".

(b)
- $R = 1.20\times10^{-15}\times197^{1/3} = 6.98\times10^{-15}\ \text{m}$ ✓

(c)
- $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{8.99\times10^{9}\times158\times(1.60\times10^{-19})^2}{6.98\times10^{-15}} = 5.21\times10^{-12}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $= 32.6\ \text{MeV}$ (accept 32–33 MeV) ✓

Allow ECF from (b). Alternative: $7.7 \times \dfrac{2.95\times10^{-14}}{6.98\times10^{-15}} = 32.5\ \text{MeV}$.

(d)
- at these energies the alpha particles reach/come within range of the nucleus ✓
- the (short-range) strong nuclear force now acts as well as the electrostatic force, so the scattering no longer follows the Coulomb-only prediction ✓

(e)
- mass $\approx Au$ and volume $= \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A$ ✓
- $\rho = \dfrac{Au}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3u}{4\pi R_0^3}$, which contains no $A$ ✓
- $\rho = \dfrac{3\times1.66\times10^{-27}}{4\pi(1.20\times10^{-15})^3} \approx 2.3\times10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ ✓

Accept use of proton or neutron mass instead of $u$ (≈ $2.3\times10^{17}$).

text:
The Bohr model gives the energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom as $E = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$.

(a) State the condition that Bohr imposed on the angular momentum of the orbiting electron. [1]

(b) Calculate the energy of the electron in the level $n = 3$. [1]

(c) An electron makes a transition from $n = 3$ to $n = 1$. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted. [2]

(d) State the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which this photon lies. [1]

(e) The radius of the $n = 1$ orbit is $5.29\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}$. Determine the speed of the electron in the $n = 2$ orbit. [3]

(f) State **one** limitation of the Bohr model. [1]
ms:
(a)
- angular momentum is quantized: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$ (with $n$ a positive integer) ✓

(b)
- $E_3 = -\dfrac{13.6}{9} = -1.51\ \text{eV}$ ✓

(c)
- $\Delta E = 13.6\left(1 - \frac{1}{9}\right) = 12.1\ \text{eV} = 1.93\times10^{-18}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{1.93\times10^{-18}} = 1.03\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}$ ✓

(d)
- ultraviolet ✓

(e)
- $r_2 = 4r_1 = 2.12\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r} = \dfrac{2\times6.63\times10^{-34}}{2\pi\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times2.12\times10^{-10}}$ ✓
- $v = 1.09\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

Alternative: speed in $n=1$ is $2.19\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v \propto 1/n$. Award [3] for correct final answer.

(f) Any one:
- only works for hydrogen/one-electron systems ✓
- cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines ✓
- does not explain why the electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate / treats the electron as a point particle in a definite orbit, inconsistent with the uncertainty principle ✓

text:
Which observation of the photoelectric effect **cannot** be explained by the wave theory of light?

A. The number of photoelectrons emitted per second increases with light intensity.
B. Photoelectrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies.
C. Below a certain frequency no photoelectrons are emitted, however intense the light.
D. Photoelectrons are emitted from metal surfaces but not from insulators.
ms: **C.** In the wave model, energy delivered to an electron grows with intensity and time, so emission should eventually occur at any frequency; a threshold frequency needs the photon model ($hf \ge \Phi$). A is consistent with both models. B arises because electrons come from different depths/energies. D is about material properties, not the nature of light.

text:
Light of wavelength 400 nm is incident on a metal surface of work function 2.3 eV.

What is the stopping potential?

A. 0.81 V
B. 2.3 V
C. 3.1 V
D. 5.4 V
ms: **A.** Photon energy $= \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.99\times10^{-25}}{4.00\times10^{-7}} = 4.97\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 3.1\ \text{eV}$; $E_\text{k,max} = 3.1 - 2.3 = 0.8\ \text{eV}$, so $V_s = 0.81\ \text{V}$. C is the photon energy; D adds the work function; B is the work function alone.

text:
An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 150 V.

What is the de Broglie wavelength of the electron?

A. $2.4\times10^{-12}\ \text{m}$
B. $5.0\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}$
C. $1.0\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}$
D. $1.4\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}$
ms: **C.** $p = \sqrt{2meV} = \sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times150} = 6.61\times10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$, $\lambda = h/p = 1.0\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}$. D results from omitting the factor 2 ($p = \sqrt{meV}$). A is the Compton wavelength $h/m_ec$, unrelated to the speed. B halves the correct answer.

text:
X-ray photons undergo Compton scattering from free electrons that are initially at rest. Three statements are made.

I. The scattered photons have a longer wavelength than the incident photons.
II. The change in wavelength depends on the wavelength of the incident photons.
III. The change in wavelength is greatest for photons scattered through 180°.

Which statements are correct?

A. I only
B. I and II only
C. II and III only
D. I and III only
ms: **D.** $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos\theta)$: the photon loses energy (I correct); $\Delta\lambda$ depends only on $\theta$, not on the incident wavelength (II wrong); $1-\cos\theta$ is maximum (= 2) at $\theta = 180°$ (III correct). Students often think II is correct because the *fractional* change depends on $\lambda$.

text:
In a photoelectric experiment, monochromatic light of frequency $f$ is shone onto a metal cathode and the stopping voltage $V_\text{s}$ is measured.

| $f$ / $10^{14}$ Hz | 6.0 | 7.0 | 8.0 | 9.0 | 10.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $V_\text{s}$ / V | 0.20 | 0.63 | 1.03 | 1.46 | 1.86 |

The data are plotted below.

![stopping voltage against frequency, five data points from 6 to 10 times 10^14 Hz](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.2_5.svg)

(a) Show that the relationship between $V_\text{s}$ and $f$ is $V_\text{s} = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{\Phi}{e}$. [1]

(b) Using the graph, determine a value for the Planck constant. [3]

(c) Determine the threshold frequency of the metal. [1]

(d) Determine the work function of the metal, in eV. [1]

(e) The intensity of the light is doubled at each frequency. State and explain the effect on the graph. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $hf = \Phi + E_\text{k,max}$ and $E_\text{k,max} = eV_\text{s}$, so $eV_\text{s} = hf - \Phi$ and dividing by $e$ gives the result ✓

(b)
- line of best fit drawn and gradient calculated using two well-separated points on the line ✓
- gradient $= \dfrac{1.86-0.20}{(10.0-6.0)\times10^{14}} \approx 4.15\times10^{-15}\ \text{V s}$ ✓
- $h = e\times\text{gradient} = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times4.15\times10^{-15} = 6.6\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ ✓

Accept gradients in the range $4.0$–$4.3\times10^{-15}\ \text{V s}$ and $h$ in the range $6.4$–$6.9\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$.

(c)
- intercept on the frequency axis: $f_0 \approx 5.5\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ (accept $5.4$–$5.6\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$) ✓

(d)
- extrapolating to the $V_\text{s}$ axis gives intercept $\approx -2.3\ \text{V}$, so $\Phi \approx 2.3\ \text{eV}$ ✓

Accept $\Phi = hf_0$ converted to eV (2.2–2.4 eV). Allow ECF from (b) and (c).

(e)
- no change to the graph / same line ✓
- $E_\text{k,max}$ depends only on photon energy (frequency) and work function; greater intensity only increases the number of photons and hence photoelectrons per second ✓

text:
(a) Describe **one** experiment that provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons. [2]

(b) An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference $V$. Its de Broglie wavelength is then 0.12 nm. Determine $V$. [3]

(c) A proton has the same de Broglie wavelength of 0.12 nm. Calculate the kinetic energy of the proton. [2]
ms:
(a)
- electrons accelerated (through a few kV) onto a thin crystalline/graphite target ✓
- a diffraction pattern of rings/maxima and minima is observed on a screen, which can only be explained by wave behaviour (spacing comparable to de Broglie wavelength) ✓

Accept the Davisson–Germer experiment: electrons scattered from a nickel crystal show intensity maxima at specific angles.

(b)
- $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{1.2\times10^{-10}} = 5.53\times10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ ✓
- $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(5.53\times10^{-24})^2}{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}} = 1.68\times10^{-17}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $V = \dfrac{E_\text{k}}{e} = 105\ \text{V}$ (accept 104–105 V) ✓

(c)
- same momentum, so $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{p^2}{2m_\text{p}} = \dfrac{(5.53\times10^{-24})^2}{2\times1.673\times10^{-27}}$ ✓
- $E_\text{k} = 9.1\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b). Award [2] for a correct final answer (≈ 0.057 eV also accepted).

text:
An X-ray photon of wavelength $7.10\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}$ is scattered by a free electron that is initially at rest. The photon is scattered through an angle $\theta = 90°$.

![Compton scattering: incident photon, scattered photon at angle theta, recoiling electron](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.2_7.svg)

(a) Calculate the wavelength of the scattered photon. [2]

(b) Determine the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron. [3]

(c) Explain how Compton scattering provides evidence that photons carry momentum. [2]

(d) Explain why the Compton effect is not readily observed with visible light. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\Delta\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos 90°) = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{9.11\times10^{-31}\times3.00\times10^{8}} = 2.43\times10^{-12}\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $\lambda' = 7.10\times10^{-11} + 0.243\times10^{-11} = 7.34\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}$ ✓

(b)
- energy conservation: $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda'}$ ✓
- $= 1.99\times10^{-25}\left(\dfrac{1}{7.10\times10^{-11}} - \dfrac{1}{7.34\times10^{-11}}\right)$ ✓
- $E_\text{k} = 9.2\times10^{-17}\ \text{J}$ (≈ 580 eV) ✓

Accept $9.0$–$9.4\times10^{-17}\ \text{J}$ owing to rounding of $\lambda'$. Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- the shift in wavelength with angle is predicted by treating the interaction as a particle collision in which both energy **and** momentum ($p = h/\lambda$) are conserved ✓
- the electron recoils/gains momentum, and the measured $\Delta\lambda$ agrees with $\dfrac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos\theta)$ ✓

(d)
- maximum shift is only about $5\times10^{-12}\ \text{m}$ (twice the Compton wavelength) ✓
- this is a tiny fraction (about $10^{-5}$) of visible wavelengths (≈ $5\times10^{-7}$ m), so it is not detectable / visible photons also have energies comparable to electron binding energies, so electrons are not free ✓

text:
Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 250 nm is incident on a clean zinc surface. The work function of zinc is 4.3 eV.

(a) Calculate the energy of one photon of this radiation, in eV. [2]

(b) Determine the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons. [3]

(c) The power of the ultraviolet radiation reaching the surface is 2.0 mW. Calculate the number of photons incident on the surface per second. [2]

(d) Explain why the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons does not change when the power of the radiation is increased. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{250\times10^{-9}} = 7.96\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $E = 4.97\ \text{eV}$ (accept 5.0 eV) ✓

(b)
- $E_\text{k,max} = 4.97 - 4.3 = 0.67\ \text{eV} = 1.08\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $\frac{1}{2}m_ev^2 = 1.08\times10^{-19}$ ✓
- $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.08\times10^{-19}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}} = 4.9\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (a). Using 5.0 eV gives $5.0\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: accept.

(c)
- $N = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{7.96\times10^{-19}}$ ✓
- $N = 2.5\times10^{15}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

(d)
- each electron absorbs the energy of only one photon, and photon energy depends only on frequency ✓
- increasing the power increases the number of photons per second (so more photoelectrons) but not the energy of each photon ✓

text:
The nuclide $^{214}_{82}\text{Pb}$ undergoes $\beta^-$ decay. What is the resulting nuclide?

A. $^{214}_{81}\text{Tl}$
B. $^{213}_{83}\text{Bi}$
C. $^{210}_{80}\text{Hg}$
D. $^{214}_{83}\text{Bi}$
ms: **D.** In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron changes into a proton (emitting an electron and an antineutrino): $Z$ increases by 1, $A$ unchanged. A is $\beta^+$ decay; C is alpha decay; B wrongly reduces $A$.

text:
A radioactive source emits a single type of radiation. The radiation passes through a sheet of paper but is almost completely stopped by 5 mm of aluminium.

Which radiation does the source emit?

A. alpha
B. beta-minus
C. gamma
D. neutrinos
ms: **B.** Beta particles penetrate paper but are stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper; gamma passes through several cm of aluminium with only partial absorption; neutrinos are virtually never stopped.

text:
The count rate from a radioactive sample, corrected for background, falls from 800 counts per minute to 50 counts per minute in 20 hours.

What is the half-life of the sample?

A. 1.25 h
B. 4.0 h
C. 5.0 h
D. 10 h
ms: **C.** 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is 4 half-lives, so $T_{1/2} = 20/4 = 5.0\ \text{h}$. A divides by 16 (the ratio, not the number of half-lives); B divides by 5 (counting the values rather than the halvings); D assumes 2 half-lives.

text:
A nucleus of $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$ undergoes one alpha decay followed by two $\beta^-$ decays. Which nuclide is produced?

A. $^{234}_{90}\text{Th}$
B. $^{234}_{94}\text{Pu}$
C. $^{234}_{92}\text{U}$
D. $^{230}_{92}\text{U}$
ms: **C.** Alpha decay: $A$ −4, $Z$ −2 → $^{234}_{90}\text{Th}$. Two $\beta^-$ decays: $Z$ +2 → $^{234}_{92}\text{U}$, an isotope of the original element. A stops after the alpha decay; B treats beta decays as adding 2 each; D subtracts too much nucleon number.

text:
The following data are available.

mass of a helium-4 nucleus $= 4.001506\ \text{u}$
mass of a proton $= 1.007276\ \text{u}$
mass of a neutron $= 1.008665\ \text{u}$

What is the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4?

A. 3.5 MeV
B. 7.1 MeV
C. 14 MeV
D. 28 MeV
ms: **B.** Mass defect $= 2(1.007276) + 2(1.008665) - 4.001506 = 0.030376\ \text{u}$; binding energy $= 0.030376\times931.5 = 28.3\ \text{MeV}$; per nucleon $= 28.3/4 = 7.1\ \text{MeV}$. D is the total binding energy; C divides by 2 (protons only); A divides by 8.

text:
Two radioactive samples X and Y initially contain the same number of undecayed nuclei. The half-life of X is $T$ and the half-life of Y is $2T$.

What is $\dfrac{\text{activity of X}}{\text{activity of Y}}$ at time $4T$?

A. $\frac{1}{4}$
B. $\frac{1}{2}$
C. 1
D. 2
ms: **B.** At $4T$: $N_X = N_0/16$, $N_Y = N_0/4$. $A = \lambda N$ with $\lambda_X = 2\lambda_Y$, so $\dfrac{A_X}{A_Y} = 2\times\dfrac{1/16}{1/4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. A is the ratio of the numbers of nuclei (ignoring $\lambda$); D is the initial activity ratio.

text:
A detector placed near a radioactive source records the count rate shown in the graph. With the source removed, the detector records a background count rate of 20 counts per minute.

![measured count rate against time, falling from about 620 towards 20 counts per minute over 20 hours](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.3_7.svg)

(a) Explain why the background count rate must be taken into account when determining the half-life from this graph. [1]

(b) Determine the half-life of the source. [3]

(c) Predict the measured count rate at $t = 12.5\ \text{h}$. [2]

(d) Suggest why repeated measurements of the count rate at the same time would not give identical values. [1]
ms:
(a)
- the measured rate includes background, which does not decay, so the source count rate is (measured − 20); halving of the measured rate does not correspond to halving of the source activity ✓

(b)
- corrected initial count rate $= 620 - 20 = 600\ \text{min}^{-1}$ ✓
- time for corrected rate to fall to 300, i.e. measured rate to reach $320\ \text{min}^{-1}$ ✓
- $T_{1/2} = 2.5\ \text{h}$ (accept 2.3–2.7 h) ✓

Award [1] max for 2.0–2.2 h obtained by halving the uncorrected rate.

(c)
- 12.5 h = 5 half-lives, so corrected rate $= 600/32 \approx 19\ \text{min}^{-1}$ ✓
- measured rate $= 19 + 20 \approx 39\ \text{min}^{-1}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b). Accept a value read directly from the graph (37–41) with reasoning.

(d)
- radioactive decay is random/spontaneous, so the number of decays in a given interval fluctuates ✓

text:
The activity $A$ of a sample of a radioactive nuclide was measured every 10 minutes. The graph shows $\ln(A/\text{Bq})$ plotted against time $t$, with the line of best fit.

![graph of ln A against time, straight line falling from 8.52 at t = 0 to about 5.34 at t = 55 min](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.3_8.svg)

(a) Explain why the graph shows that the decay is exponential. [2]

(b) Determine the decay constant of the nuclide, in $\text{s}^{-1}$. [2]

(c) Calculate the half-life of the nuclide. [1]

(d) Determine the number of undecayed nuclei in the sample at $t = 0$. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $A = A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ gives $\ln A = \ln A_0 - \lambda t$ ✓
- this is of the form $y = c + mx$, so a straight line with negative gradient ($-\lambda$) confirms exponential decay ✓

(b)
- gradient $= \dfrac{5.34 - 8.52}{55 - 0} = -0.0578\ \text{min}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = 0.0578\ \text{min}^{-1}$ ✓
- $\lambda = \dfrac{0.0578}{60} = 9.6\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept $\lambda$ in the range $9.3$–$9.9\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

(c)
- $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = 720\ \text{s} = 12\ \text{min}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- $A_0 = e^{8.52} \approx 5.0\times10^{3}\ \text{Bq}$ ✓
- $N_0 = \dfrac{A_0}{\lambda} = \dfrac{5.0\times10^{3}}{9.6\times10^{-4}} = 5.2\times10^{6}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b).

text:
Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope that decays by $\beta^-$ emission.

(a) Complete the equation for the decay of carbon-14, identifying all the particles produced. [2]

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + \ldots + \ldots$$

(b) Compare the ionizing ability and the penetrating power of the beta particles emitted by carbon-14 with those of alpha particles. [2]

(c) The graph shows the region of stable nuclides on a plot of neutron number $N$ against proton number $Z$. Two unstable nuclides, X and Y, are marked.

![neutron number against proton number with band of stable nuclides; X above the band, Y below](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.3_9.svg)

Deduce the most likely mode of decay for X and for Y. [2]

(d) State **two** properties of the strong nuclear force. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$ ✓
- $+\ \bar{\nu}_e$ (electron antineutrino) ✓

Do not accept neutrino (instead of antineutrino) for the second mark.

(b)
- beta particles are less (strongly) ionizing than alpha particles ✓
- beta particles are more penetrating: stopped by a few mm of aluminium rather than by paper/a few cm of air ✓

(c)
- X has too many neutrons for stability, so it decays by $\beta^-$ emission ✓
- Y has too few neutrons (too many protons), so it decays by $\beta^+$ emission (or electron capture) ✓

(d) Any two:
- very short range (≈ $10^{-15}$ m) ✓
- strongly attractive between nucleons at typical separations / repulsive at very short separations ✓
- acts equally between protons and neutrons (independent of charge) ✓
- much stronger than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances ✓

text:
Iodine-131, used in medicine, has a half-life of 8.02 days. A sample of iodine-131 has an activity of $4.0\times10^{6}\ \text{Bq}$ when it is delivered to a hospital.

(a) Calculate the decay constant of iodine-131, in $\text{s}^{-1}$. [2]

(b) Calculate the number of iodine-131 nuclei in the sample when it is delivered. [1]

(c) Determine the mass of iodine-131 in the sample. [2]

(d) Calculate the activity of the sample 30.0 days after delivery. [2]

(e) The sample is considered unusable when its activity falls below $1.0\times10^{5}\ \text{Bq}$. Determine, in days, how long after delivery this occurs. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{8.02\times24\times3600}$ ✓
- $\lambda = 1.00\times10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

(b)
- $N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{4.0\times10^{6}}{1.00\times10^{-6}} = 4.0\times10^{12}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- mass of one nucleus $\approx 131\times1.66\times10^{-27} = 2.17\times10^{-25}\ \text{kg}$ ✓
- total mass $= 4.0\times10^{12}\times2.17\times10^{-25} = 8.7\times10^{-13}\ \text{kg}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b).

(d)
- $A = 4.0\times10^{6}\,e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda t = 1.00\times10^{-6}\times30.0\times86400 = 2.59$ ✓
- $A = 3.0\times10^{5}\ \text{Bq}$ ✓

Alternative: $A = 4.0\times10^{6}\times(0.5)^{30.0/8.02}$.

(e)
- $\ln\left(\dfrac{4.0\times10^{6}}{1.0\times10^{5}}\right) = \lambda t$, so $t = \dfrac{\ln 40}{\lambda} = 3.69\times10^{6}\ \text{s}$ ✓
- $t = 42.7$ days (accept 43 days) ✓

text:
Polonium-210 decays by alpha emission to an isotope of lead. The polonium nucleus is initially at rest.

| particle | atomic mass / u |
|---|---|
| polonium-210 | 209.982874 |
| lead-206 | 205.974465 |
| helium-4 | 4.002603 |

(a) Write down the nuclear equation for this decay. [1]

(b) Show that the energy released in the decay is about 5.4 MeV. [2]

(c) Determine the kinetic energy of the alpha particle. [3]

(d) Polonium-210 is a very serious hazard if swallowed or inhaled, but a sealed sample presents little hazard from outside the body. Explain this difference. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow\ ^{206}_{82}\text{Pb} + {}^{4}_{2}\alpha$ (or ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$) ✓

(b)
- mass defect $= 209.982874 - (205.974465 + 4.002603) = 0.005806\ \text{u}$ ✓
- $E = 0.005806\times931.5 = 5.41\ \text{MeV}$ ✓

Atomic masses may be used because the electron numbers balance (84 = 82 + 2).

(c)
- momentum conservation: lead and alpha have equal and opposite momenta, $p_\text{Pb} = p_\alpha$ ✓
- $E_\text{k} = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $\dfrac{E_\alpha}{E_\text{Pb}} = \dfrac{m_\text{Pb}}{m_\alpha} = \dfrac{206}{4}$ ✓
- $E_\alpha = 5.41\times\dfrac{206}{210} = 5.30\ \text{MeV}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (b). Award [1] max for 5.41 MeV with the statement that the lead is much heavier.

(d)
- alpha particles have a very short range/are stopped by a few cm of air, paper or the outer dead layer of skin, so they do not reach living cells from outside the body ✓
- inside the body they are strongly ionizing and deposit all their energy in a small volume of living tissue, damaging cells/DNA ✓

text:
What is the function of the moderator in a thermal nuclear fission reactor?

A. To absorb neutrons so that the rate of fission is controlled
B. To reflect neutrons back into the core to reduce the critical mass
C. To transfer thermal energy from the core to the heat exchanger
D. To slow down neutrons so that they are more likely to cause fission
ms: **D.** The moderator slows fast neutrons by collisions so they become thermal neutrons, which are much more likely to be captured by uranium-235 and cause fission. A describes the control rods; C describes the coolant; B describes a reflector.

text:
A possible fission reaction of uranium-235 is

$$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow\ ^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + x\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$$

What is $x$?

A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 4
ms: **C.** Nucleon number: $235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + x$, so $x = 3$ (proton numbers also balance: 92 = 56 + 36). B forgets the incoming neutron on the left-hand side.

text:
The binding energy per nucleon of uranium-235 is about 7.6 MeV. The fission products of uranium-235 have a binding energy per nucleon of about 8.5 MeV.

What is the approximate energy released when one uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission?

A. 0.9 MeV
B. $2\times10^{2}$ MeV
C. $1.8\times10^{3}$ MeV
D. $2.0\times10^{3}$ MeV
ms: **B.** Energy released ≈ (increase in binding energy per nucleon) × (number of nucleons) $= (8.5 - 7.6)\times235 \approx 210\ \text{MeV}$. A forgets to multiply by the number of nucleons; C and D are the total binding energies of the reactant and products, not the difference.

text:
A nuclear reactor produces thermal power of 1.0 GW. Each fission of uranium-235 releases 200 MeV.

What is the approximate mass of uranium-235 that undergoes fission each day?

A. 0.044 kg
B. 1.1 kg
C. 2.6 kg
D. $4.5\times10^{-3}$ kg
ms: **B.** Energy per fission $= 200\times1.60\times10^{-13} = 3.2\times10^{-11}\ \text{J}$; fissions per second $= 10^{9}/3.2\times10^{-11} = 3.1\times10^{19}\ \text{s}^{-1}$; per day $= 2.7\times10^{24}$ nuclei; mass $= 2.7\times10^{24}\times235\times1.66\times10^{-27} \approx 1.1\ \text{kg}$. A is the mass per hour; C wrongly divides by an efficiency of 40 % (the power given is already thermal); D uses the mass of one nucleon (1 u) instead of the mass of a uranium-235 nucleus.

text:
The graph shows how the binding energy per nucleon varies with nucleon number $A$ for a number of nuclides.

![binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, peak near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.4_5.svg)

(a) Identify, with reference to the graph, the regions of nucleon number in which energy can be released by fission and by fusion. [2]

(b) A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two fragments of approximately equal nucleon number, releasing two neutrons. Use the graph to estimate the energy released. [3]

(c) Use the graph to estimate the energy released when two deuterium (hydrogen-2) nuclei fuse to form a helium-4 nucleus. [2]

(d) Using your answers to (b) and (c), compare the energy released per unit mass of fuel in fission and in fusion. [1]
ms:
(a)
- fission: heavy nuclei to the right of the peak (A greater than about 60, in practice $A \gtrsim 200$) split into nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon ✓
- fusion: light nuclei to the left of the peak ($A$ less than about 60, in practice very light nuclei) combine to give higher binding energy per nucleon ✓

(b)
- fragments have $A \approx 117$, with binding energy per nucleon ≈ 8.5 MeV; U-235 ≈ 7.6 MeV ✓
- energy released ≈ $234\times8.5 - 235\times7.6$ ✓
- ≈ 200 MeV (accept 180–230 MeV) ✓

Accept the approximation $235\times(8.5-7.6)$.

(c)
- binding energy of He-4 ≈ $4\times7.1 = 28.3\ \text{MeV}$; of two H-2 ≈ $2\times2\times1.1 = 4.4\ \text{MeV}$ ✓
- energy released ≈ 24 MeV (accept 22–25 MeV) ✓

(d)
- fusion: ≈ 24 MeV/4 u ≈ 6 MeV per nucleon; fission: ≈ 200 MeV/236 u ≈ 0.85 MeV per nucleon, so fusion releases several (≈ 7) times more energy per unit mass ✓

Allow ECF from (b) and (c).

text:
The diagram is a simplified outline of a thermal nuclear fission reactor.

![reactor outline with fuel rods, part P lowered from above, Q surrounding the fuel, coolant loop to heat exchanger R](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.4_6.svg)

(a) Identify the parts labelled P, Q and R. [3]

(b) Outline what is meant by a chain reaction in the reactor. [2]

(c) Explain how the operator would reduce the power output of the reactor. [2]

(d) State **one** problem associated with the waste produced by the reactor. [1]
ms:
(a)
- P: control rods ✓
- Q: moderator (e.g. graphite or water) ✓
- R: heat exchanger (steam generator) ✓

(b)
- each fission of a U-235 nucleus releases two or three neutrons ✓
- these neutrons go on to cause further fissions, so the reaction is self-sustaining ✓

(c)
- insert/lower the control rods further into the core ✓
- they absorb more neutrons, so fewer neutrons are available to cause fission and the fission rate decreases ✓

(d) Any one:
- fission products are highly radioactive with long half-lives, requiring secure storage for thousands of years ✓
- spent fuel generates heat and must be cooled ✓
- plutonium in spent fuel could be used for nuclear weapons ✓

text:
A fission reaction in a uranium reactor is

$$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow\ ^{144}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{89}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$$

| particle | mass / u |
|---|---|
| uranium-235 | 235.043930 |
| barium-144 | 143.922953 |
| krypton-89 | 88.917631 |
| neutron | 1.008665 |

(a) Show that the energy released in one fission is about 170 MeV. [3]

(b) Calculate the energy released when 1.0 kg of uranium-235 undergoes fission in this way. [2]

(c) The barium-144 and krypton-89 nuclei are radioactive. Suggest why. [2]

(d) A power station using this reaction has an electrical output of 600 MW and an overall efficiency of 35 %. Estimate the mass of uranium-235 that undergoes fission in one year. [3]
ms:
(a)
- mass of reactants $= 235.043930 + 1.008665 = 236.052595\ \text{u}$; mass of products $= 143.922953 + 88.917631 + 3\times1.008665 = 235.866579\ \text{u}$ ✓
- mass defect $= 0.186016\ \text{u}$ ✓
- $E = 0.186016\times931.5 = 173\ \text{MeV}$ ✓

(b)
- number of nuclei in 1.0 kg $= \dfrac{1.0}{235\times1.66\times10^{-27}} = 2.56\times10^{24}$ ✓
- $E = 2.56\times10^{24}\times173\times1.60\times10^{-13} = 7.1\times10^{13}\ \text{J}$ ✓

Allow ECF from (a).

(c)
- fission fragments have a neutron-to-proton ratio similar to uranium, which is too high for stable nuclei of their mass ✓
- so they are neutron-rich and decay (by $\beta^-$ emission) towards stability ✓

(d)
- input power $= \dfrac{600}{0.35} = 1.71\times10^{9}\ \text{W}$ ✓
- energy per year $= 1.71\times10^{9}\times3.16\times10^{7} = 5.4\times10^{16}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- mass $= \dfrac{5.4\times10^{16}}{7.1\times10^{13}} \approx 760\ \text{kg}$ (accept 700–800 kg) ✓

Allow ECF from (b).

text:
In a thermal reactor, neutrons released by fission have kinetic energies of about 2 MeV. They must be slowed to about 0.025 eV by collisions with the nuclei of a moderator.

(a) Explain why the neutrons need to be slowed down. [1]

(b) A neutron of mass $m$ makes a head-on elastic collision with a stationary carbon-12 nucleus of mass $12m$. Show that the neutron retains a fraction $\left(\frac{11}{13}\right)^2$ of its kinetic energy. [3]

(c) Estimate the number of such head-on collisions needed to reduce the energy of a neutron from 2 MeV to 0.025 eV. [2]

(d) Water is also used as a moderator. Suggest why fewer collisions are needed with hydrogen nuclei than with carbon nuclei. [2]
ms:
(a)
- slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission than fast neutrons ✓

(b)
- momentum: $mu = mv + 12mV$ ✓
- kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}(12m)V^2$ ✓
- solving gives $v = -\frac{11}{13}u$, so fraction of KE retained $= \left(\frac{v}{u}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{11}{13}\right)^2$ ✓

Accept use of relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation ($u = V - v$) in place of the energy equation.

(c)
- $\left(\frac{11}{13}\right)^{2n} = \dfrac{0.025}{2\times10^{6}} = 1.25\times10^{-8}$ ✓
- $n = \dfrac{\ln(1.25\times10^{-8})}{\ln 0.716} \approx 55$ ✓

Accept 54–55. Award [1] max for a trial-and-error answer without a valid method.

(d)
- the mass of a hydrogen nucleus (proton) is almost equal to that of the neutron ✓
- so in a head-on collision the neutron can transfer (nearly) all its kinetic energy / loses a much larger fraction per collision ✓

text:
A main-sequence star is in stable equilibrium. Which forces are balanced?

A. Gravitational force inwards and radiation and gas pressure forces outwards
B. Gravitational force inwards and the strong nuclear force outwards
C. Electrostatic repulsion between nuclei and gravitational force
D. Magnetic force inwards and radiation pressure force outwards
ms: **A.** Hydrostatic equilibrium: the inward gravitational pull on the outer layers is balanced by the outward pressure (gas and radiation) produced by energy released from fusion in the core. B and C confuse nuclear-scale forces with the forces acting on the star as a whole; D is not the main balance.

text:
Star X has twice the radius of the Sun and half the surface temperature of the Sun.

What is $\dfrac{\text{luminosity of X}}{\text{luminosity of the Sun}}$?

A. $\frac{1}{8}$
B. $\frac{1}{4}$
C. 1
D. 4
ms: **B.** $L = \sigma4\pi R^2T^4$, so the ratio $= 2^2\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \frac{4}{16} = \frac{1}{4}$. A uses $R$ instead of $R^2$; C uses $T^2$; D ignores temperature.

text:
The parallax angle of a star is 0.020 arc-seconds. What is the distance to the star?

A. $6.2\times10^{14}\ \text{m}$
B. $4.7\times10^{17}\ \text{m}$
C. $1.5\times10^{18}\ \text{m}$
D. $1.5\times10^{19}\ \text{m}$
ms: **C.** $d = 1/p = 1/0.020 = 50\ \text{pc} = 50\times3.09\times10^{16} = 1.5\times10^{18}\ \text{m}$. A multiplies $p$ by the parsec instead of dividing; B treats 50 as light-years; D has a power-of-ten error.

text:
Stars X and Y have the same apparent brightness. X is twice as far from Earth as Y, and the surface temperature of X is twice that of Y.

What is $\dfrac{\text{radius of X}}{\text{radius of Y}}$?

A. $\frac{1}{8}$
B. $\frac{1}{4}$
C. $\frac{1}{2}$
D. 2
ms: **C.** $b = \dfrac{L}{4\pi d^2}$ with equal $b$ gives $L_X = 4L_Y$. $L \propto R^2T^4$, so $R_X^2\times16 = 4R_Y^2$ and $R_X/R_Y = \frac{1}{2}$. B is $R^2$ ratio (forgetting the square root); D ignores the temperature; A uses $d$ instead of $d^2$ and forgets the root.

text:
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen occurs in the core of a star. Which conditions are needed for fusion to take place at a significant rate?

I. A very high temperature so that nuclei can overcome their electrostatic repulsion
II. A very high density so that collisions between nuclei are frequent
III. A low pressure so that the strong nuclear force can act over large distances

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** High temperature gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to come close enough (≈ $10^{-15}$ m) for the strong force to act; high density makes collisions frequent. III is wrong: the strong force always has a very short range, and core pressure is very high.

text:
The Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram shows a number of stars, including the Sun and stars labelled P, Q and X. Luminosity is given in units of the Sun's luminosity $L_\odot$.

![HR diagram with main sequence, giants, white dwarfs; Sun at 5800 K, P at 4000 K and 10^4 solar luminosities, Q at 20000 K and 10^4, X at 12000 K and 0.003](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.5_6.svg)

(a) State the type of star represented by
(i) P. [1]
(ii) X. [1]

(b) The surface temperature of the Sun is 5800 K. Use the diagram to determine $\dfrac{R_\text{P}}{R_\odot}$, the radius of P in terms of the radius of the Sun. [3]

(c) Q and the Sun are both main-sequence stars. Outline why Q will spend a much shorter time on the main sequence than the Sun. [2]

(d) State the final stage in the evolution of the Sun. [1]
ms:
(a)(i)
- red supergiant (accept red giant) ✓

(a)(ii)
- white dwarf ✓

(b)
- from the diagram: $L_\text{P} = 10^{4}L_\odot$ and $T_\text{P} = 4000\ \text{K}$ ✓
- $L \propto R^2T^4$ so $\dfrac{R_\text{P}}{R_\odot} = \sqrt{\dfrac{L_\text{P}}{L_\odot}}\times\left(\dfrac{T_\odot}{T_\text{P}}\right)^2$ ✓
- $= 100\times\left(\dfrac{5800}{4000}\right)^2 \approx 210$ ✓

Accept 190–230 for readings of T between 3800 K and 4200 K.

(c)
- Q is more massive and so has a much greater luminosity / rate of fusion ✓
- its luminosity increases much faster with mass than its supply of hydrogen, so it uses up the hydrogen in its core much faster ✓

(d)
- white dwarf (after a red giant and planetary nebula stage) ✓

text:
The diagram (not to scale) illustrates how the distance $d$ to a nearby star can be measured using stellar parallax.

![stellar parallax: Earth in January and July either side of the Sun, nearby star with parallax angle p, distant stars behind](qbank/img/gen_phys_E.5_7.svg)

(a) Define the parsec. [1]

(b) Explain why the position of the nearby star appears to change relative to the distant stars when observed in January and in July. [2]

(c) The parallax angle $p$ of the star is 0.125 arc-seconds. Calculate the distance to the star in metres. [2]

(d) Suggest why the parallax method can only be used for relatively nearby stars. [1]
ms:
(a)
- the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arc-second (the distance to a star with parallax angle of 1 arc-second) ✓

(b)
- the Earth is at opposite sides of its orbit, so the star is viewed from two different positions (2 AU apart) ✓
- the nearby star is much closer than the distant stars, so its direction changes by a much larger angle; the distant stars act as a fixed background ✓

(c)
- $d = \dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{1}{0.125} = 8.0\ \text{pc}$ ✓
- $d = 8.0\times3.09\times10^{16} = 2.5\times10^{17}\ \text{m}$ ✓

(d)
- for distant stars the parallax angle is too small to be measured accurately ✓

text:
A star has an apparent brightness of $1.0\times10^{-7}\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ and is at a distance of 190 pc from Earth. The peak of its emission spectrum is at a wavelength of 830 nm.

(a) Calculate the surface temperature of the star. [2]

(b) Show that the luminosity of the star is about $4\times10^{31}\ \text{W}$. [2]

(c) Determine the radius of the star. [3]

(d) The luminosity of the Sun is $3.8\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$ and its radius is $7.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m}$. Identify, with reasons, the type of star. [2]

(e) Predict the final stage in the evolution of this star. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $T = \dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{\lambda_\text{max}} = \dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{830\times10^{-9}}$ ✓
- $T = 3.5\times10^{3}\ \text{K}$ ✓

(b)
- $d = 190\times3.09\times10^{16} = 5.87\times10^{18}\ \text{m}$ ✓
- $L = 4\pi d^2b = 4\pi(5.87\times10^{18})^2\times1.0\times10^{-7} = 4.3\times10^{31}\ \text{W}$ ✓

(c)
- $L = \sigma4\pi R^2T^4$ ✓
- $R = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.3\times10^{31}}{4\pi\times5.67\times10^{-8}\times(3.5\times10^{3})^4}}$ ✓
- $R = 6.4\times10^{11}\ \text{m}$ (accept $6.2$–$6.6\times10^{11}\ \text{m}$) ✓

Allow ECF from (a) and (b).

(d)
- $L \approx 10^{5}L_\odot$ and $R \approx 900R_\odot$ ✓
- very luminous, very large and cool (red) so it is a red supergiant ✓

Allow ECF from (c).

(e)
- supergiants are massive stars that end in a (core-collapse) supernova ✓
- leaving a neutron star or a black hole (depending on the mass of the remnant core) ✓

text:
In the core of the Sun, hydrogen is converted to helium. The overall reaction can be written as

$$4\,{}^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow\ {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{1}\text{e}^{+} + 2\nu_e$$

mass of a proton $= 1.007276\ \text{u}$
mass of a helium-4 nucleus $= 4.001506\ \text{u}$
mass of a positron $= 0.000549\ \text{u}$

(a) Calculate the energy released in this reaction. Ignore the mass of the neutrinos. [3]

(b) Each positron annihilates with an electron, so the total energy released per helium nucleus formed is 26.7 MeV. The luminosity of the Sun is $3.8\times10^{26}\ \text{W}$. Determine the mass of hydrogen converted into helium in the Sun each second. [2]

(c) When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core contracts. Explain why this causes the core temperature to rise. [2]

(d) Outline why fusion reactions in stars do not produce elements heavier than iron as a significant energy source. [2]

(e) Compare the final stages of evolution of a star of 1 solar mass and a star of 15 solar masses. [3]
ms:
(a)
- mass defect $= 4\times1.007276 - 4.001506 - 2\times0.000549$ ✓
- $= 0.026500\ \text{u}$ ✓
- $E = 0.026500\times931.5 = 24.7\ \text{MeV}$ ✓

Award [2] max for 26.7 MeV unless the student explicitly includes annihilation.

(b)
- number of reactions per second $= \dfrac{3.8\times10^{26}}{26.7\times1.60\times10^{-13}} = 8.9\times10^{37}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓
- mass of hydrogen $= 4\times1.67\times10^{-27}\times8.9\times10^{37} = 5.9\times10^{11}\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$ ✓ (accept $5.9$–$6.0\times10^{11}$ kg s$^{-1}$)

(c)
- as the core contracts, gravitational potential energy decreases ✓
- this energy is transferred to the kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature rises (until helium fusion can start) ✓

(d)
- the binding energy per nucleon is a maximum near iron/nickel ✓
- fusing nuclei to form elements heavier than iron decreases the binding energy per nucleon, so energy must be supplied rather than released ✓

(e)
- 1 solar mass: red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf ✓
- 15 solar masses: red supergiant → supernova ✓
- leaving a neutron star or black hole, because the core mass exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit (≈ 1.4 solar masses), while the Sun's remnant core is below it ✓
